questions.stem: A day can only be cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is $0.5$, independent of the condition on other days. What is the probability that in any given four days, there will be three cloudy days and one sunny day?

steps.title: Independent events and counting outcomes
steps.body: Two events are independent when one does not change the chance of the other. Here each day is cloudy with probability $0.5$ whatever the other days were. For independent days, the probability of one particular sequence (say cloudy, cloudy, cloudy, sunny) is the product of the single-day probabilities. The question asks for the pattern (three cloudy, one sunny) in any order, so we add up the probabilities of all sequences that fit the pattern.

steps.title: Probability of one sequence
steps.body: A sequence with 3 cloudy days and 1 sunny day multiplies four factors of $0.5$, so every such sequence has the same probability.

steps.title: Count the sequences
steps.body: The single sunny day can fall on day 1, 2, 3 or 4, giving 4 sequences: SCCC, CSCC, CCSC, CCCS. This is the number of ways to choose which 1 of 4 days is sunny.

steps.title: Add and match
steps.body: The 4 sequences cannot happen together, so their probabilities add: $4 \times \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. This is option (A).

shortcut.body: Four fair flips give $2^4 = 16$ equally likely sequences. "Exactly one sunny" can sit in 4 positions, so $4/16 = 1/4$ in about 20 seconds.

traps.text: Taking $3/4$ because three of the four days are cloudy. That is the fraction of cloudy days in the pattern, not the probability of getting the pattern.
Taking $2/3$, which no count of equally likely sequences can give. Every sequence of four days has probability $1/16$, so the answer must be a multiple of $1/16$.
Taking $3/8 = 6/16$, which is the probability of exactly two cloudy days, $\binom{4}{2}/16$. The wrong binomial coefficient swaps one sunny day for two.

recognize.clues: Each day has two outcomes with equal chance and the days are independent. The question asks for a fixed number of cloudy days "in any given four days", so order does not matter.
recognize.contrast: This is not a conditional probability question: nothing is given about one day that changes another. It is also not a single fixed sequence, because every placement of the sunny day counts.

check.body: The four days have 16 equally likely weather sequences. The counts by number of sunny days are 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, which add to 16, so the cases are complete. The row with exactly one sunny day holds 4 sequences, and 4 out of 16 reproduces the result.

questions.stem: The values of Stock A and Stock B on a particular day are Rs. 50 and Rs. 80, respectively. An investor invests Rs. 100 in Stock A and Rs. 80 in Stock B. He sells all the stocks the next day when the value of Stock A is Rs. 55 and Stock B is Rs. 70. The profit made by the investor is Rs. ________

steps.title: Profit means selling value minus buying value
steps.body: Profit is what you receive on selling minus what you paid. A negative profit is a loss. A holding is a number of units; the money paid is units times the price per unit, and the money received is units times the new price. So we first find how many units of each stock the investor owns.

steps.title: Units of each stock
steps.body: Rs. 100 buys $100/50 = 2$ units of Stock A at Rs. 50. Rs. 80 buys $80/80 = 1$ unit of Stock B at Rs. 80.

steps.title: Gain or loss per stock
steps.body: Stock A moves from 50 to 55, a gain of 5 per unit, so $2 \times 5 = +10$. Stock B moves from 80 to 70, a loss of 10 per unit, so $1 \times (-10) = -10$.

steps.title: Total and option
steps.body: The gain on A cancels the loss on B, so the profit is Rs. 0. This is option (A).

shortcut.body: Compute each stock separately: A gives $+5$ on each of 2 units $= +10$, B gives $-10$ on one unit. They cancel to 0, so pick (A). Check: sale $110+70 = 180$ equals the amount invested $100+80 = 180$.

traps.text: Reading the per-unit rise of Stock A ($55-50 = 5$) as the profit, ignoring that Rs. 100 buys 2 units and that Stock B lost money.
Counting only Stock A's gain of Rs. 10 and ignoring the loss on Stock B.
Adding the gain of A ($10$) to the drop of B as if it were a gain ($+10$), which ignores the sign: $10 + 10 = 20$.

recognize.clues: Two investments with different amounts and prices, and a single profit asked for after both prices move. The words "invests Rs. 100 in Stock A" give money, not units.
recognize.contrast: Do not compare per-unit prices directly, as in a percentage-change question on one item. Here the number of units differs between the stocks, so each gain must be weighted by its units before adding.

check.body: Work in percentage returns. Stock A rose from 50 to 55, which is $+10\%$ on Rs. 100, so $+10$. Stock B fell from 80 to 70, which is $-12.5\%$ on Rs. 80, so $-10$. The two returns cancel.

questions.stem: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the sum of the two recorded numbers is a prime number is ________

steps.title: Probability by counting equally likely outcomes
steps.body: When all outcomes are equally likely, probability is (favourable outcomes) divided by (all outcomes). Two rolls of a six-faced die give $6 \times 6 = 36$ ordered outcomes, each equally likely. A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. The sum of two dice lies between 2 and 12, so the primes to look for are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.

steps.title: Count the ways to make each prime
Divide and match
steps.body: Favourable outcomes are 15 out of 36, which is option (C).

shortcut.body: Remember the two-dice sum counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 for sums 2 to 12. Pick the prime sums: $1+2+4+6+2 = 15$. Answer $15/36$ in under a minute. Do not forget that 2 is prime.

traps.text: Counting only the prime sums 2 and 3 ($1+2 = 3$ ways) and stopping before 5, 7 and 11.
Dropping the sum 11, which has 2 ways ((5,6) and (6,5)), so the count is 13 instead of 15.
Treating 9 as prime and adding its 4 ways to the correct 15. But $9 = 3 \times 3$.

recognize.clues: A fair die rolled twice gives equally likely outcomes, and the event is described by a property of the sum (it is prime). That points to counting favourable pairs over 36.
recognize.contrast: This is not a conditional or Bayes question: no outcome is given in advance. It also is not the multiples question, where the condition compares the two rolls instead of testing their sum.

check.body: The counts of ordered pairs for the sums 2 to 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and they add to 36, so the table is complete. Second route by complement: the composite sums 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 have 3, 5, 5, 4, 3, 1 pairs, which is 21 pairs. Then 36 minus 21 leaves 15 pairs with a prime sum, the same count as before.

questions.stem: Consider a knock-out women's badminton singles tournament where there are no ties. The loser in each game is eliminated from the tournament. Every player plays until she is defeated or remains the last undefeated player. The last undefeated player is declared the winner of the tournament. If there are 64 players in the beginning of the tournament, how many games should be played in total to declare the winner of the tournament?

steps.title: Knock-out rule: one loser per game
steps.body: In a knock-out tournament with no ties, every game produces exactly one loser, and a loser leaves for good. The tournament ends when exactly one player has not lost. So the number of games equals the number of players who must be eliminated, because games and eliminations match one for one.

steps.title: Count eliminations
steps.body: Start with 64 players and end with 1 undefeated player, so $64 - 1 = 63$ players must lose a game. Each game removes one player.

steps.title: Cross-check with rounds
steps.body: Round by round: $32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 63$ games. The two methods agree, so the answer is option (C).

shortcut.body: Games $=$ players $- 1$ in any knock-out with no byes and no replays. $64-1=63$. 15 seconds. The shortcut holds whatever the bracket shape.

traps.text: Choosing $127$ by summing $64+32+16+8+4+2+1$. The 64 counts players, not games; round one has only 32 games.
Choosing $64$, the number of players. The winner is never eliminated, so only 63 players lose.
Choosing $32$, which is the number of games in the first round only.

recognize.clues: Knock-out, no ties, loser eliminated, and one undefeated winner at the end. Each game has exactly one loser, so games and eliminations match one for one.
recognize.contrast: A round-robin tournament, where every pair plays once, needs $\binom{n}{2}$ games. Here a player stops after one defeat, so the count is linear in the number of players, not quadratic.

check.body: Every game has exactly one loser, so the number of games equals the number of losers. Test the idea on small fields: 2 players need 1 game, and 4 players need 3 games (two semi-finals and a final). Each time, games are one fewer than players, and the same holds for any field size, with or without byes.

questions.stem:
For positive real numbers $S$ and $K$, the function $H_K(S)$ is defined as: $H_K(S) = \max(S - K, 0)$. The max function is defined as:

$\max(a,b) = a$ when $a > b$, and $b$ when $a \le b$.

The graph below shows the plot of a function $N(S)$ versus $S$.

$N(S)$ can be expressed as ______.
questions.figure: A plot of N(S) against S for S from 0 to 30 (horizontal gridlines at N = 0, 2, 4, ..., 12; vertical at S = 0, 10, 20, 30). N(S) = 0 from S = 0 to S = 10, then a straight line rises from (10, 0) to (20, 10), then N(S) stays at 10 up to S = 30.

diagram.alt: Plot of N(S) against S: zero up to S = 10, a straight rise to 10 at S = 20, then flat at 10 up to S = 30

solutionDiagram.alt: Dashed line H10(S) and dotted line H20(S) drawn with the plotted N(S) in bold: subtracting H20(S) from H10(S) flattens the rise at S = 20

steps.title: What H_K(S) looks like
steps.body: $H_K(S) = \max(S-K, 0)$ is zero while $S \le K$ and equals $S-K$ once $S > K$. Its graph is flat at 0, then bends at $S = K$ and climbs with slope 1. The point $K$ is the kink. When functions are added or subtracted, their slopes add or subtract, so each $H_K$ switches on a slope of $+1$ at its own $K$ and leaves it on.

steps.title: Read the kinks and slopes of N(S)
steps.body: From the graph, $N(S)$ is 0 up to $S=10$, then climbs from 0 to 10 over $S$ from 10 to 20, a slope of $+1$. After $S = 20$ it is flat, so the slope returns to 0. So the slope turns on ($+1$) at 10 and turns off (a change of $-1$) at 20.

steps.title: Build it from hinge functions
steps.body: $H_{10}(S)$ turns on slope $+1$ at 10. To switch the slope back to 0 at 20, subtract a function that turns on slope $+1$ at 20, that is $H_{20}(S)$. So $N(S) = H_{10}(S) - H_{20}(S)$.

steps.title: Check by values
steps.body: At $S = 15$: $5 - 0 = 5$, on the line. At $S = 20$: $10 - 0 = 10$. At $S = 30$: $20 - 10 = 10$, flat at 10. All match the plot, so the answer is option (A).

shortcut.body: Test the value at $S = 30$ where the plot reads 10: (A) gives $20-10=10$; (B) gives $20-20=0$; (C) gives $-20+10=-10$; (D) gives $15-10=5$. Only (A) matches, in about 40 seconds.

traps.text: Subtracting $2H_{20}$ makes the slope $-1$ after $S=20$, so $N$ would fall back to 0 at $S=30$ instead of staying at 10.
Reversing the signs gives a graph that falls below zero. The plot never goes negative, so $-H_{10}+H_{20}$ cannot be it.
Putting the first kink at 15 instead of 10. At $S=15$ this option gives 0, but the plot already reads 5 there.

recognize.clues: A piecewise linear graph with a flat start, one straight rise and a flat end, together with functions built from $\max(S-K,0)$. Read the kinks off the plot and match them to the $K$ values.
recognize.contrast: This is not a data-interpretation table question. The slope changes of the plot carry the information, so identify where each hinge switches on rather than reading single values.

check.body: Test points the solution did not use: one on the rising line, one beyond the second kink, one below the first. The expression must give the line height at 12, the flat height at 25, and 0 at 8.

questions.stem: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the number appearing in the second roll is an integer multiple of the number appearing in the first roll is __________

steps.title: Multiples and equally likely outcomes
steps.body: A number $b$ is an integer multiple of $a$ when $b = k a$ for some whole number $k$, that is, when $a$ divides $b$. The two rolls give $36$ equally likely ordered pairs $(a, b)$, so probability is (favourable pairs)/36. For each first roll $a$ we count how many values $b$ in $1..6$ are multiples of $a$.

steps.title: Count for each first roll
steps.body: $a=1$: all 6 values. $a=2$: 2, 4, 6, which is 3. $a=3$: 3, 6, which is 2. $a=4$: only 4, which is 1. $a=5$: only 5, 1. $a=6$: only 6, 1. In general the count is $\lfloor 6/a \rfloor$.

steps.title: Divide and match
steps.body: There are 14 favourable pairs out of 36, so $14/36 = 7/18$, option (C).

shortcut.body: For each first roll $a$, the favourable second rolls number $\lfloor 6/a\rfloor$: $6,3,2,1,1,1$. Total 14, over 36, gives $7/18$. About a minute.

traps.text: Counting only the first roll 1, which gives 6 pairs out of 36. Larger first rolls also have multiples, and every number is a multiple of itself.
Undercounting by 4 pairs, giving $10/36 = 5/18$, for example by leaving out (2,4), (2,6), (3,6) and (2,2). The right count is 14.
Computing $5/6$, which is the chance that the two rolls differ. It has nothing to do with divisibility.

recognize.clues: Two independent fair rolls with a divisibility relation between them. The relation is between the first and second roll, so fix the first roll and count the second rolls that satisfy it.
recognize.contrast: This differs from a sum or product condition, where the event depends on a single combined value. Here the condition is asymmetric, so (2,4) is favourable but (4,2) is not.

check.body: The condition is asymmetric, so count it a second way: for each second roll count how many first rolls divide it. The divisor counts of 1 to 6 are 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4 and this reaches the same favourable total as the row-by-row count.

questions.stem: If $Pe^{x} = Qe^{-x}$ for all real values of $x$, which one of the following statements is true?

steps.title: What "for all real x" demands
steps.body: An equation that must hold for every real $x$ is an identity: both sides must be the same function. The exponential $e^{x}$ is always positive and grows without bound as $x$ increases; $e^{-x}$ is always positive and shrinks towards 0. Their ratio $e^{x}/e^{-x} = e^{2x}$ changes with $x$, so no single constant ratio can link them. The rule: if $P e^{2x}$ equals the constant $Q$ for all $x$, then $P e^{2x}$ cannot vary, which forces $P = 0$.

steps.title: Reduce the equation
steps.body: Multiply both sides by $e^{x}$, which is never zero, to get $Pe^{2x} = Q$ for all $x$. The right side is constant. The left side is constant only when $P = 0$, since $e^{2x}$ takes different values at $x=0$ and $x=1$.

steps.title: Find Q
steps.body: With $P = 0$ the left side is 0, so $Q = 0$. Check: $0\cdot e^{x} = 0\cdot e^{-x}$ is true for every $x$.

steps.title: Compare with the options
steps.body: $P = Q = 0$ is option (A). Option (D) says $P/Q = 0$, which needs $Q \ne 0$ and $P = 0$. But the equation with $P = 0$ forces $Q = 0$, a contradiction, so (D) is false for every pair $(P, Q)$, not merely incomplete.

shortcut.body: Plug in two values. At $x = 0$: $P = Q$. At $x = 1$: $Pe = Q/e$, so with $P = Q$ we get $P(e - 1/e) = 0$ and $P = 0$. Hence $P = Q = 0$. About 45 seconds.

traps.text: Taking $P=Q=1$ because $x=0$ gives $P=Q$. That single point is satisfied by $P=Q=1$, but the equation fails at $x=1$ since $e \ne 1/e$.
Choosing $P=1,\ Q=-1$ makes the equation $e^{x}=-e^{-x}$, which is false at $x=0$ because $1 \ne -1$.

Reading $P/Q=0$ as "P is zero" and accepting it. The ratio is $0$ only if $P=0$ and $Q\ne 0$, yet $P=0$ forces $Q=0$ in the equation. So (D) is false for every pair $(P,Q)$; when $Q=0$ the ratio is undefined.

recognize.clues: The phrase "for all real values of $x$" together with $e^{x}$ and $e^{-x}$. The two exponentials are never equal for $x\ne0$, so the identity can only hold when both coefficients vanish.
recognize.contrast: This is not an equation to solve for a particular $x$. Satisfying it at $x=0$ alone, which only gives $P=Q$, is much weaker than satisfying it for every $x$.

check.body: Substitute $P=Q=0$: both sides are 0 for every $x$, so the identity holds. Now try $P=Q=1$ at $x=1$: the left side is $e$ and the right side is $1/e$, and $e\ne1/e$, so it fails.

questions.stem: Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ denote two arbitrary prime numbers. Which one of the following statements is correct for all values of $p_1$ and $p_2$?
options: $p_1 + p_2$ is not a prime number.
$p_1 p_2$ is not a prime number.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. A number with another divisor, such as a product of two numbers each greater than 1, is composite. A statement "correct for all values" fails if even one example breaks it, so we test small primes: 2, 3, 5, 7.

steps.title: The product of two primes
steps.body: The number $p_1 p_2$ is divisible by $p_1$, and $1 < p_1 < p_1 p_2$ because $p_2 > 1$. So $p_1p_2$ has a divisor other than 1 and itself and is always composite, whatever the primes are, including $p_1 = p_2$.
steps.tex: p_1 \mid p_1 p_2,\quad 1 < p_1 < p_1 p_2

steps.title: Break the other three
steps.body: (A): $2 + 3 = 5$ is prime. (C): $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$ is not prime. (D): $3 \times 3 + 1 = 10$ is not prime. Each fails for some choice, so only (B) holds for all primes.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: Option (B) is correct.

shortcut.body: The product of two numbers greater than 1 is composite, so (B) is true by definition. Confirm by killing the rest with 2 and 3: $2+3=5$, $2+3+1=6$, $3\cdot3+1=10$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Assuming the sum of two primes is even because primes are odd. $2+3=5$ is prime, because one of the primes can be 2.
Testing only $2+2+1=5$ and $3+3+1=7$, which are prime, and stopping. One counter-example, $2+3+1=6$, kills the claim.
Testing $2\cdot 2+1=5$ and $2 \cdot 3+1=7$, which are prime, and not testing $3\cdot 3+1=10$.

recognize.clues: Arbitrary primes and a statement that must hold "for all values". This is a counter-example and divisibility argument on small integers.

steps.title: A recurrence rule from a table
steps.body: A recurrence says each output is built from the previous output and an input. To find which rule fits, take a row of the table, look at how the output moved from step $i-1$ to step $i$, and test whether it was a sum or a product with the input. steps.title: Match

recognize.contrast: A plain number series has no separate input row; here the input changes every step, so you must test sum against product with the current input, not look for a fixed difference or ratio.

questions.stem:
In the given figure, PQRS is a square of side 2 cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of the rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square.

What is the area (in $\text{cm}^2$) of the rectangle PLMN?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.figure: Square PQRS of side 2 cm with P top left, Q bottom left, R bottom right, S top right. Point L lies on side QR. A rectangle PLMN has vertices in order P, L, M, N, with M to the lower right of the square and N above S. Side MN passes through the corner S of the square. Side PL runs inside the square from P to L.

diagram.alt: Square PQRS of side 2 cm with rectangle PLMN: L on side QR, side MN passing through S

solutionDiagram.alt: Triangle PLS shaded: base PS = 2, height 2, area 2, half of rectangle PLMN so the rectangle has area 4

steps.title: Area facts we need
steps.body: The area of a triangle is half of base times height. The area of a rectangle is its two adjacent sides multiplied. A triangle that shares a side of a rectangle and whose third corner lies on the opposite side has exactly half the rectangle's area, because its base is the shared side and its height is the distance between the two parallel sides.

steps.title: Find the triangle inside the rectangle
steps.body: Take triangle PLS. Its base is PL, a side of the rectangle. The corner S lies on side MN, which is opposite and parallel to PL. The distance from S to line PL equals LM, the other side of the rectangle. So the triangle has base PL and height LM.

steps.title: Compute the triangle a second way
steps.body: Use PS as the base instead. P and S are the top corners of the square, so PS = 2. L is on the bottom side QR, which is 2 below PS. So the height is 2, whatever the position of L on QR.

steps.title: Double it
steps.body: The rectangle is twice the triangle: $2 \times 2 = 4$ cm$^2$. This is option (D). A coordinate check with $P=(0,2)$, $L=(1,0)$, $S=(2,2)$ gives $|\overrightarrow{PL}\times\overrightarrow{PS}| = 4$ as well, and the value does not change as L slides along QR.

shortcut.body: The rectangle is twice triangle PLS, and that triangle has base PS = 2 and height 2 (L is on the opposite side of the square), so it has area 2 and the rectangle has area 4. Slide L to Q or R mentally to confirm it does not matter. About 90 seconds.

traps.text: Using the diagonal of the square, $2\sqrt2$, as if it were a side of the rectangle. The diagonal PR is not a side of PLMN.
Taking the triangle PLS area (2) as the rectangle's area. The triangle is only half of the rectangle.
Multiplying base 2 by height 4 (or doubling the area twice). The rectangle is exactly twice the triangle of area 2, no more.

recognize.clues: A square with a rectangle tilted inside it, L free on a side, and the rectangle's side passing through the corner S. The free point signals that the area must come out the same wherever L is, which suggests a triangle-half-of-rectangle argument.
recognize.contrast: Mensuration problems give the rectangle's sides directly. Here the sides are unknown, so you find area through the triangle PLS instead of multiplying length by width.

check.body: Test the two extreme positions of L. With L at Q the rectangle is the strip with sides 2 and 2, area 4. With L at R the side PL is the diagonal $2\sqrt2$ and the width is the distance from S to that diagonal, $\sqrt2$, so the area is again $2\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=4$.

questions.stem:
The diagram below shows a river system consisting of 7 segments, marked P, Q, R, S, T, U, and V. It splits the land into 5 zones, marked Z1, Z2, Z3, Z4, and Z5. We need to connect these zones using the least number of bridges. Out of the following options, which one is correct?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.figure: A rectangular map with a river system. The river enters from the left edge as segment P and meets a junction. From this junction a branch goes up to the top edge as segment R, and a branch goes right as segment Q to a second junction. From the second junction a branch goes down-left to the bottom edge as segment S, and the river continues right as segment T to a third junction. From the third junction a branch goes up-right to the right edge as segment V and another goes down-right to the right edge as segment U. Zone Z2 is in the top left, between P and R. Zone Z3 is in the top middle, bounded by R, Q, T and V. Zone Z1 is in the bottom left, bounded by P, Q and S. Zone Z5 is in the bottom middle, bounded by S, T and U. Zone Z4 is on the right, between V and U.
options: Bridges on P, Q, and T
Bridges on P, Q, S, and T
Bridges on Q, R, T, and V
Bridges on P, Q, S, U, and V

diagram.alt: River map with segments P, Q, R, S, T, U, V cutting the land into zones Z1 to Z5

solutionDiagram.alt: Zones as dots and river segments as links between the zones they separate; bridges on Q, R, T, V (thick) connect all five zones with four bridges

steps.title: Zones, segments and what a bridge does
steps.body: Think of each zone as a dot. A river segment separates two zones, so a bridge on that segment joins the two dots. To reach every zone from every other, the dots must form one connected group. With $n$ dots, at least $n - 1$ links are needed. Here $n = 5$, so the least number of bridges is 4.

steps.title: Read which zones each segment separates
steps.body: P separates Z1 and Z2. R separates Z2 and Z3. Q separates Z1 and Z3. T separates Z3 and Z5. S separates Z1 and Z5. V separates Z3 and Z4. U separates Z4 and Z5.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: (A) has 3 bridges for 5 zones, below the minimum of 4, so it cannot connect them. (B) P, Q, S, T join Z1, Z2, Z3, Z5 but nothing reaches Z4. (C) Q joins Z1-Z3, R joins Z2-Z3, T joins Z3-Z5, V joins Z3-Z4, so all five zones meet at Z3 through 4 bridges. (D) connects everything but uses 5 bridges, not the least.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: Only option (C) connects all zones with the least number of bridges.

shortcut.body: The least number of bridges for 5 zones is 4, which removes (A) (only 3) and (D) (5). Between (B) and (C), look for the one that touches Z4: only V or U can, and only (C) has V. About 90 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing the shortest option, with 3 bridges. Three links can join at most 4 zones, so one zone is left cut off.
Choosing four bridges that never touch Z4. Count which zones each option reaches, not just how many bridges it has.
Choosing a set that does connect all zones but has 5 bridges. The question asks for the least number.

recognize.clues: A map with labelled river segments and zones, and the phrase least number of bridges. The words connect and least point to reading the map as a connection structure between regions.
recognize.contrast: A map-reading question about distances or directions needs scale; here only which regions touch matters, so you reduce the map to zones and links.

check.body: In option (C) the four bridges join Z3 to each of Z1, Z2, Z5 and Z4, so there is no loop. Removing any one bridge cuts a zone off, which shows none of the four can be spared and 4 is truly the least.

questions.stem: The average marks obtained by a class in an examination were calculated as 30.8. However, while checking the marks entered, the teacher found that the marks of one student were entered incorrectly as 24 instead of 42. After correcting the marks, the average becomes 31.4. How many students does the class have?

steps.title: Average means total divided by count
steps.body: The average (mean) of $n$ numbers is their total divided by $n$. So total $=$ average $\times$ $n$. When one entry is corrected, the number of students $n$ is unchanged and only the total changes, by (correct value $-$ wrong value). The new average is the new total divided by the same $n$.

steps.title: Change in the total
steps.body: The mark was entered as 24 but should have been 42. The total rises by $42 - 24 = 18$.

steps.title: Change in the average
steps.body: The average rises from 30.8 to 31.4, a rise of $0.6$. The rise in total divided by $n$ is the rise in average.

shortcut.body: Only the change matters: total up by 18, average up by 0.6, so $n = 18/0.6 = 30$. No need to use 30.8 itself. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 25 after taking the total change as 15. With $n=25$ the average would rise by $18/25 = 0.72$, not 0.6.
Choosing 28 from a rounding slip in $18/0.6$. Test any option by multiplying: $0.6 \times 28 = 16.8 \ne 18$.
Choosing 32 by estimating. With $n=32$ the average would rise by $18/32 \approx 0.56$, not 0.6.

recognize.clues: Two averages for the same class, a single entry corrected, and a question about the number of students. The unchanged count and the changed total are the signal.
recognize.contrast: Weighted-average problems merge groups of different sizes. Here there is one group, so no weights are needed, only the shift in total over the fixed count.

check.body: The old total $30.8n$ must be a whole number. Since $30.8=154/5$, $n$ has to be a multiple of 5. Among the options only 25 and 30 qualify, and 25 gives a rise of $18/25=0.72$ while 30 gives $0.6$.

questions.stem:
In the diagram, the lines QR and ST are parallel to each other. The shortest distance between these two lines is half the shortest distance between the point P and line QR. What is the ratio of the area of the triangle PST to the area of the trapezium SQRT?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.figure: Triangle PQR with P at the top, Q at the bottom left and R at the bottom right. Point S lies on side PQ and point T lies on side PR. The segment ST is parallel to the base QR. The trapezium SQRT is the part of the triangle below ST.

diagram.alt: Triangle PQR with line ST parallel to base QR, cutting the triangle into triangle PST and trapezium SQRT

solutionDiagram.alt: ST sits halfway up the height h, so triangle PST is similar to PQR at half scale: area 1 unit out of 4, trapezium 3 units

steps.title: Similar triangles and their areas
steps.body: Two triangles are similar when they have the same angles; then every length in one is the same multiple $k$ of the matching length in the other. Their areas then differ by the factor $k^2$, because area has two length dimensions. A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle cuts off a smaller triangle with the same angles, so it is similar to the whole.

steps.title: Find the scale factor
steps.body: Let the height of $P$ above $QR$ be $h$. The distance between ST and QR is $h/2$, so the distance from P to ST is also $h/2$. Triangle PST has height $h/2$ and triangle PQR has height $h$, so $k = 1/2$.

steps.title: Compare areas
steps.body: $[PST] = k^2 [PQR] = \tfrac14[PQR]$. The trapezium is what remains of the big triangle: $[SQRT] = [PQR] - [PST] = \tfrac34 [PQR]$.

steps.title: Ratio and match
steps.body: The ratio is $\tfrac14 : \tfrac34 = 1 : 3$, which is option (A).

shortcut.body: Half the height means a half-scale triangle, so area $1/4$ of the whole. The trapezium is the other $3/4$, and the ratio is $1:3$. About 40 seconds. Do not halve the area: areas scale as the square.

traps.text: Giving $1/4$, which is the area of PST compared with the whole triangle, not compared with the trapezium.
Giving $2/5$ by guessing a ratio from lengths such as $2:3$. The ratio of sides is $1:2$, and areas follow the square of that.
Giving $1/2$ by using the length ratio directly as the area ratio. Area scales with the square of the scale factor.

recognize.clues: A line ST parallel to the base QR, a given ratio of distances, and a question about areas of the cut-off triangle and the trapezium. Parallel lines with distance ratios point to similar triangles.
recognize.contrast: Mensuration asks for an area from given lengths. Here no length is given, only ratios, so similarity and the squared scale factor replace the area formula.

check.body: Put numbers on it with $Q=(0,0)$, $R=(6,0)$ and $P=(3,6)$, so $h=6$ and ST lies at height 3 with length 3. The small triangle has area $\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot3=4.5$, the trapezium has area $\tfrac{6+3}{2}\cdot3=13.5$, and $4.5/13.5=1/3$.

questions.stem: A fair six-faced dice, with the faces labelled '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', and '6', is rolled thrice. What is the probability of rolling '6' exactly once?

steps.title: Independent rolls and "exactly once"
steps.body: Rolls of a fair die are independent, so the chance of a specific sequence is the product of the single-roll chances. A six has probability $1/6$ and a non-six has probability $5/6$. "Exactly once" means one roll shows 6 and the other two do not, in any order, so we add the sequences that fit.

steps.title: One sequence
steps.body: For the sequence six, non-six, non-six the probability is $\tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac56 \cdot \tfrac56 = \tfrac{25}{216}$. The same product appears for each position of the six.

steps.title: Count the positions
steps.body: The six can be on roll 1, 2 or 3, so there are 3 sequences, $\binom31 = 3$. They cannot happen together, so add.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: $75/216$ is option (A). It simplifies to $25/72$.

shortcut.body: Use the binomial form $\binom31 (1/6)(5/6)^2 = 3\cdot25/216 = 75/216$. Option (D) is a single sequence, so the answer must be 3 times it. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Giving $1/6$, the chance of a six on one roll. It ignores the other two rolls.
Giving $1/18$, which is $(1/6)\cdot(1/3)$ and has no meaning here. The answer must be a count times $25/216$.
Giving $25/216$, the probability of one fixed order. The six can be on any of the 3 rolls, so multiply by 3.

recognize.clues: A fair die rolled several times with a count condition, exactly once. Independent repeated trials with a fixed success chance on each roll mark a binomial count.
recognize.contrast: A single-roll event uses just the favourable over total faces. Here several rolls are combined, so you multiply per sequence and then count sequences instead of using one fraction.

check.body: The four possible counts of sixes in three rolls must have probabilities summing to 1. Using $\binom3k(1/6)^k(5/6)^{3-k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$ gives $125,75,15,1$ over 216, which add to 216 over 216.

questions.stem: A shop has 4 distinct flavors of ice-cream. One can purchase any number of scoops of any flavor. The order in which the scoops are purchased is inconsequential. If one wants to purchase 3 scoops of ice-cream, in how many ways can one make that purchase?

steps.title: Choosing with repeats and no order
steps.body: Here the same flavor may be picked several times, and only how many scoops of each flavor matter, not the order. Such a selection is a multiset. The count of multisets of size $r$ from $n$ kinds is the number of non-negative whole-number solutions to $x_1 + \dots + x_n = r$, where $x_i$ is the number of scoops of flavor $i$.

steps.title: Stars and bars
steps.body: Write the 3 scoops as 3 stars and use $n - 1 = 3$ bars to split them among the 4 flavors. Each arrangement of 3 stars and 3 bars is one purchase, and there are $3 + 3 = 6$ positions of which we pick 3 for stars.

steps.title: Compute and verify by cases
steps.body: $\binom63 = 20$. By cases: all 3 scoops of one flavor gives 4 ways; two of one flavor and one of another gives $4 \times 3 = 12$ ways; three different flavors gives $\binom43 = 4$ ways. Total $4 + 12 + 4 = 20$.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: The count is 20, which is option (B).

shortcut.body: Multiset formula: $\binom{n+r-1}{r} = \binom{6}{3} = 20$. About 30 seconds. Use the case split (4, 12, 4) as a check if time is left.

traps.text: Counting only the purchases of 3 scoops of the same flavor (4 ways), ignoring mixed purchases.
Counting ordered choices of three different flavors, $4\cdot3\cdot2 = 24$. Order does not matter, and repeats are allowed.
Computing $4 \times 12 = 48$ from only the "two of one, one of another" case, with the wrong factor. With no order, the count is much lower.

recognize.clues: Distinct flavors, any number of scoops of any flavor, and order is inconsequential. Repeats allowed with no order is the multiset pattern.
recognize.contrast: Ordinary combinations forbid repeats and arrangements count order. Here repeats are allowed and order is ignored, so neither $\binom43$ nor $4^3$ applies.

check.body: Test the formula on a smaller case you can list. With 4 flavors and 2 scoops it gives $\binom52=10$, and listing gives 4 purchases of one flavor twice plus 6 purchases of two different flavors, also 10.

questions.stem:
Two wizards try to create a spell using all the four elements, water, air, fire, and earth. For this, they decide to mix all these elements in all possible orders. They also decide to work independently. After trying all possible combination of elements, they conclude that the spell does not work.

How many attempts does each wizard make before coming to this conclusion, independently?

steps.title: What is being counted
steps.body: An order of the elements is a way of writing them one after another, such as water, air, fire, earth. Two orders are different when at least one position holds a different element, so water, air, fire, earth and air, water, fire, earth are two separate attempts. When $n$ different items are each used exactly once, the number of orders is built by the multiplication rule: choose the item for the first position, then for the second, and so on, and multiply the number of choices at each position. The word "independently" means each wizard works through the full list alone, so we count one wizard only.

steps.title: Fill the four positions
steps.body: The first position can hold any of the 4 elements. Once one is used, 3 remain for the second position, then 2 for the third, and the last position is forced.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Each wizard tries all 24 orders before concluding that no order works. That is option (A). The number for both wizards together would be $2 \times 24 = 48$, which is not what is asked.

shortcut.body: Four different items in all possible orders is $4! = 24$. The question asks about one wizard, so no doubling. About 15 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 48 by counting both wizards together, $2 \times 24$. The question asks how many attempts each wizard makes.
Choosing 16, which treats each of the 4 positions as having only 2 choices ($2^4$) or multiplies $4 \times 4$. Each element must be used exactly once, so the choices shrink 4, 3, 2, 1.

Choosing 12, which is $4!/2$, treating an order and its mirror image as the same attempt, or stops the product after two positions ($4 \times 3$). Every distinct order is a separate attempt, and all four positions are filled.

recognize.clues: All four elements used, in all possible orders. Using every item once with order mattering is a count of permutations of distinct items.
recognize.contrast: A selection where order is ignored uses combinations. Here a different order is a different attempt, so the count is a factorial, not a binomial coefficient.

check.body: Count by fixing the first element instead. Each of the 4 choices for the first element leaves the other three to be ordered in $3!=6$ ways, so the total is $4\cdot6=24$.

questions.stem:
In an engineering college of 10,000 students, 1,500 like neither their core branches nor other branches. The number of students who like their core branches is 1/4th of the number of students who like other branches. The number of students who like both their core and other branches is 500.

The number of students who like their core branches is

solutionDiagram.alt: Venn diagram of 10,000 students: core only 1,300, both 500, other branches only 6,700, neither 1,500, so core total is 1,800 and other-branches total is 7,200

steps.title: Sets, overlap and the rule for a union
steps.body: Let $C$ be the group of students who like their core branch and $O$ the group who like other branches. A student can be in both groups, and the 500 who like both sit inside $C$ and also inside $O$. The union is the group of students in at least one of the two. When you add the size of $C$ to the size of $O$, the students in the overlap are counted twice, so one copy of the overlap is subtracted. That gives the rule below. Everyone is either in the union or in neither, so union plus "neither" equals the whole college.

steps.title: Find the union
steps.body: The college has 10,000 students and 1,500 are in neither group, so the union is the rest.

steps.title: Write the other facts with one unknown
steps.body: Let $c = |C|$ be the number we want. The statement "core is $1/4$ of other" says $c = |O|/4$, so $|O| = 4c$. The overlap is 500. Put these into the rule from step 1.

steps.title: Solve and check
steps.body: Then $5c = 9000$, so $c = 1800$ and $|O| = 7200$. Check by splitting into four non-overlapping parts: core only $1800 - 500 = 1300$, both 500, other only $7200 - 500 = 6700$, and neither 1500. They add to $1300 + 500 + 6700 + 1500 = 10000$. The answer is option (A).

shortcut.body: Union $= 10000 - 1500 = 8500$. Test an option $c$ in $c + 4c - 500 = 8500$: for 1,800 this is $9000 - 500 = 8500$, a match. Option 3,500 is out at once because $4 \times 3500 = 14000$ exceeds the college. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing 3,500. Then the other-branches group would have $4 \times 3500 = 14000$ students, more than the whole college. Plugging an option back in exposes this.
Choosing 1,600, which comes from adding the overlap, $c + 4c + 500 = 8500$, instead of subtracting it. The overlap is counted twice in $|C| + |O|$, so it must be taken off once.
Choosing 1,500, which is only the number who like neither, copied from the statement. Plugging in $c = 1500$ gives a union of $1500 + 6000 - 500 = 7000$ and 3,000 in neither, not 1,500.

recognize.clues: Three counts of students are given (neither, both, a one-fourth relation) over a total of 10,000. Words such as "neither" and "both" point to a union with an overlap.
recognize.contrast: This is counting with a union rule, not a chance question, even though it sits with the probability topic. Do not add the two groups without removing the overlap, which would count the 500 twice.

check.body: Split the college into four non-overlapping parts using the found sizes: core only, both, other only and neither. Their sum must be the whole college. Also confirm that core is one-fourth of the other-branches group.

questions.stem: For positive non-zero real variables $x$ and $y$, if $\ln\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left[\ln(x) + \ln(y)\right]$ then, the value of $\frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{x}$ is

steps.title: The logarithm rules
steps.body: The natural logarithm $\ln$ turns products into sums, $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$, and a multiplier in front into a power, $k \ln a = \ln(a^k)$. It is also one-to-one for positive numbers: if $\ln A = \ln B$ then $A = B$, because $\ln$ keeps rising and never repeats a value. So we turn the right side into a single logarithm, then drop $\ln$ from both sides.

steps.title: Combine the right side
steps.body: Half of a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of the square root of the product.

steps.title: Drop the logarithm and solve
steps.body: The two logarithms are equal, so their insides are equal: $\frac{x+y}{2} = \sqrt{xy}$. Square both sides and clear the fraction. A perfect square equal to zero forces $x = y$.

steps.title: Evaluate the expression
steps.body: Since $x = y$ and both are positive, each ratio is 1, so the sum is $1 + 1 = 2$. That is option (C).

shortcut.body: The equation says the arithmetic mean of $x, y$ equals their geometric mean, and that happens only when $x = y$ (AM-GM equality). Then $x/y + y/x = 2$. Test: $x = y = 5$ gives $\ln 5 = \tfrac12(2\ln 5)$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 1, which is the value of one ratio, $x/y = 1$. The expression asks for the sum of two ratios, $x/y + y/x$.
Choosing $1/2$ by carrying the $\tfrac12$ from the equation into the answer. The $\tfrac12$ only turns the sum of logarithms into a square root.
Choosing 4 by writing $x^2 + y^2 = 4xy$. Expanding $(x+y)^2 = 4xy$ gives $x^2 + y^2 + 2xy = 4xy$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 2xy$ and the ratio sum is 2.

recognize.clues: The equation has natural logarithms of a mean on one side and half the sum of two logarithms on the other. That shape asks for the product and power rules, then equal insides.
recognize.contrast: It also looks like an AM-GM inequality, but here the two means are set equal, which is the equality case and forces $x = y$. An inequality would give a range instead of one value.

check.body: Substitute a pair with $x = y$, for example $x = y = 5$, into the original equation, and compute the target. Then try a pair with $x \ne y$ such as 2 and 8 to see the equation fail.

questions.stem: A person sold two different items at the same price. He made 10% profit in one item, and 10% loss in the other item. In selling these two items, the person made a total of

steps.title: What profit and loss percentages are measured on
steps.body: The cost price $CP$ is what the person paid and the selling price $SP$ is what he got. Profit is $SP - CP$ when positive and loss is $CP - SP$ when positive. A profit or loss percentage is always measured on the cost price of that item. So "10% profit" means $SP = 1.10\,CP$ and "10% loss" means $SP = 0.90\,CP$. The same 10% is therefore a different number of rupees on the two items, because their cost prices differ. The overall percentage is total gain or loss over the total cost price.

steps.title: Choose a convenient selling price
steps.body: Let each item sell for Rs 99, a number that divides by 1.1 and 0.9 neatly. The profit item cost $99/1.1 = 90$. The loss item cost $99/0.9 = 110$.

steps.title: Total over the two items
steps.body: Together he paid $90 + 110 = 200$ and received $99 + 99 = 198$. He received 2 less than he paid.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The loss is 1% of the total cost price, option (C). The loss item has the larger cost price (110 against 90), so its 10% loss in rupees (11) is bigger than the 10% profit in rupees (9). That is why the net result is a loss.

shortcut.body: Equal selling prices with the same percentage $x$ on gain and on loss always give a net loss of $x^2/100$ percent: $10^2/100 = 1\%$ loss. Unsafe if the two selling prices differ or the percentages differ; then use the $SP = 99$ style check.

traps.text: Choosing 1% profit by assuming the profit item matters more. The loss item cost more (110 against 90), so the loss in rupees is the larger one.
Choosing 2% profit, which gets both the size and the sign wrong: the net amount is Rs 2 on Rs 200, which is 1%, and it is a loss.
Choosing 2% loss by reading the net amount, Rs 2, as a percentage. A percentage needs the base: $2/200 = 1\%$.
Saying the gain and loss cancel and the total is 0%. They would cancel only if the 10% were taken on the same cost price, but here the selling price is the same, so the cost prices differ.

recognize.clues: Two items have the same selling price but opposite percentage changes of the same size. Profit and loss percentages are tied to cost price, which is different for the two items.
recognize.contrast: Successive percentage changes on one quantity multiply, which is a different situation. Here there are two separate items, so you total rupees first and take the percentage at the end.

check.body: Repeat with a different selling price, such as 198. The cost prices scale together with the selling price, so the net percentage must come out the same. This confirms that the result does not depend on the price chosen.

questions.stem:
The pie charts depict the shares of various power generation technologies in the total electricity generation of a country for the years 2007 and 2023.

The renewable sources of electricity generation consist of Hydro, Solar and Wind. Assuming that the total electricity generated remains the same from 2007 to 2023, what is the percentage increase in the share of the renewable sources of electricity generation over this period?
questions.figure: Two pie charts side by side. Year 2007: Coal 35%, Gas 25%, Wind 5%, Hydro 30%, Solar 5%. Year 2023: Coal 20%, Gas 15%, Wind 10%, Hydro 35%, Solar 20%. In each chart the five shares add to 100%.

diagram.alt: Two pie charts of electricity generation shares: 2007 has Coal 35, Gas 25, Wind 5, Hydro 30, Solar 5 percent; 2023 has Coal 20, Gas 15, Wind 10, Hydro 35, Solar 20 percent

solutionDiagram.alt: Stacked bars of the renewable share: 2007 is Hydro 30 plus Solar 5 plus Wind 5 equals 40; 2023 is Hydro 35 plus Solar 20 plus Wind 10 equals 65; rise of 25 over 40 is 62.5 percent

steps.title: Reading a pie chart and the word "increase"
steps.body: A pie chart splits one whole into sectors, and each label is that sector's share of the whole, so the shares in one chart add to 100%. Because the total electricity is the same in 2007 and 2023, a 5% share in one year and a 5% share in the other stand for the same amount of electricity, and the shares can be compared directly. Two different words matter. A change of shares from 40% to 65% is a rise of 25 percentage points. The percentage increase is that change divided by the starting value: $(\text{new} - \text{old})/\text{old} \times 100$.

steps.title: Add up the renewable shares
steps.body: Renewables are Hydro, Solar and Wind. In 2007: $30 + 5 + 5 = 40$. In 2023: $35 + 20 + 10 = 65$. As a check, the non-renewables (Coal, Gas) are $35 + 25 = 60$ in 2007 and $20 + 15 = 35$ in 2023, and $40 + 60 = 65 + 35 = 100$.

steps.title: Percentage increase on the 2007 value
steps.body: The share rose by $65 - 40 = 25$ points, measured against the starting share of 40. That is option (D).

shortcut.body: Sum the three renewable slices in each pie: 40 and 65. Increase $= 25/40 = 5/8 = 62.5\%$. Divide by the old value, not by 100 and not by the new value. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 25%, the rise in percentage points. That is the raw difference of the shares; the question asks for the increase relative to the 2007 share of 40.

Choosing 50%, which comes from counting only the new sources, Solar and Wind, as the rise: $(10 + 20) - (5 + 5) = 20$ points, and $20/40 = 50\%$. That leaves out the 5-point rise in Hydro, from 30 to 35, which is renewable too, so the true rise is 25 points.
Choosing 77.5%. This is a distractor: no single misreading of the charts gives it, and it sits near the true 62.5% only to tempt a guess. Computing $25/40$ exactly avoids it.
Dividing the 25-point rise by the 2023 share, $25/65 = 38.5\%$. The percentage increase uses the starting (2007) value as its base.

recognize.clues: Two pie charts of shares are given for two years with the total fixed, and the question asks for a percentage increase in a combined group of sectors. This asks for a read-off, a sum and a relative change.
recognize.contrast: This is not a plain percentage-points question. A rise of the share by some points is not the same number as the percentage increase over the old share.

check.body: Use a second route through the non-renewable shares. They fall from 60 to 35, so the renewable share rose by the same 25 points that the others lost. Then apply the increase to the 2007 renewable share and see that it reaches the 2023 share.

questions.stem: If two distinct non-zero real variables $x$ and $y$ are such that $(x + y)$ is proportional to $(x - y)$ then the value of $\frac{x}{y}$
options: depends only on $x$ and not on $y$
depends only on $y$ and not on $x$

steps.title: What "proportional" means
steps.body: Saying $A$ is proportional to $B$ means $A = kB$ for one fixed number $k$, the constant of proportionality. The number $k$ does not change when $x$ and $y$ change; it is set by the problem. To decide what $x/y$ depends on, solve for $x/y$ and see which letters are left. If only $k$ is left, the ratio is a constant.

steps.title: Write the relation
steps.body: Because $x \ne y$, the number $x - y$ is not zero, and $k$ is a fixed non-zero constant.

steps.title: Solve for the ratio
steps.body: Divide both sides by $y$ (allowed, $y \ne 0$) and write $t = x/y$. Collect the $t$ terms on one side. The case $k = 1$ would give $y = 0$, which is excluded, so $k \ne 1$.

steps.title: Read off the dependence
steps.body: The answer contains only $k$, no $x$ and no $y$ on their own, so $x/y$ is a constant. Example with $k = 3$: $(x, y) = (2, 1)$ gives $3 = 3 \times 1$ and $(4, 2)$ gives $6 = 3 \times 2$, and the ratio is $2$ both times. That is option (D).

shortcut.body: Componendo and dividendo: $\frac{x+y}{x-y} = k$ gives $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{k+1}{k-1}$ in one line, a number fixed by $k$. Or try $k = 3$ with $(2,1)$ and $(4,2)$ and see the same ratio. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing "depends on $xy$". The product $xy$ never appears; the ratio comes out as $(k+1)/(k-1)$.
Choosing "depends only on $x$". Pairs $(2,1)$ and $(4,2)$ have different $x$ and the same ratio, so $x$ does not decide it.
Choosing "depends only on $y$". The pairs $(2,1)$ and $(6,3)$ have different $y$ and the same ratio, so $y$ does not decide it either.

recognize.clues: The wording "is proportional to" between two expressions in $x$ and $y$ means one fixed multiplier. The question then asks what the ratio $x/y$ depends on.
recognize.contrast: Direct proportion of a variable to another variable would make $x/y$ equal to $k$. Here two combinations $x + y$ and $x - y$ are proportional, so the ratio comes out as $(k+1)/(k-1)$ instead of $k$.

check.body: Go backwards from a chosen ratio. Pick $x/y = 3$, say $x = 3$, $y = 1$. Then $x + y = 4$ and $x - y = 2$, so the multiplier is $k = 2$, and the formula gives back the same ratio.

questions.stem:
Consider the following sample of numbers:

9, 18, 11, 14, 15, 17, 10, 69, 11, 13

The median of the sample is

steps.title: What the median is
steps.body: The median is the middle value of the data after it is sorted from smallest to largest, so half the values lie below it and half above. With an odd number of values it is the single middle one. With an even number of values there are two middle values, and the median is their average. Because the median depends on position, not size, one extreme value such as 69 does not move it. The mean (sum divided by count) and the mode (the most frequent value) are different measures.

steps.title: Sort the sample
steps.body: There are 10 values. In order they are 9, 10, 11, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 69.

steps.title: Average the two middle values
steps.body: With 10 values the middle sits between the 5th and 6th. The 5th is 13 and the 6th is 14.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The median is 13.5, option (A). For comparison, the mean is $187/10 = 18.7$, pulled up by 69, and the mode is 11.

shortcut.body: Cross out the smallest and the largest value, then the next smallest and next largest, and so on: 9 and 69, 10 and 18, 11 and 17, 11 and 15. Two values remain, 13 and 14, and the median is 13.5. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 14, the 6th value, by rounding the middle position 5.5 up. With an even count the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values.
Choosing 11, which is the mode, the value that appears twice. The question asks for the median.
Choosing 18.7, which is the mean. The single large value 69 drags the mean up, which is exactly why the median is used for such data.

recognize.clues: The word "median" with an unsorted list that has one very large value, 69. Median depends on position after sorting, so that value does not shift it.
recognize.contrast: The mean uses every value and is pulled up by 69, and the mode is the value that repeats. Check which of these the question names before reading off a number.

check.body: Count the sorted values on each side of the proposed median. There must be exactly five values at or below it and five at or above it. Also confirm that the single large value does not change the middle pair.

questions.stem: The number of coins of ₹1, ₹5, and ₹10 denominations that a person has are in the ratio 5:3:13. Of the total amount, the percentage of money in ₹5 coins is

steps.title: A ratio of counts is not a ratio of money
steps.body: A ratio $5:3:13$ means the person has $5k$, $3k$ and $13k$ coins for some common multiplier $k$. The amount of money in one kind of coin is the number of coins times the value of one coin. The question asks for a share of money, so each count must first be multiplied by its denomination. The percentage is the money in ₹5 coins divided by the total money, times 100.

steps.title: Money in each kind of coin
steps.body: Take $k = 1$, since $k$ cancels in a share. The ₹1 coins are worth $5 \times 1 = 5$, the ₹5 coins $3 \times 5 = 15$, and the ₹10 coins $13 \times 10 = 130$. The total is $5 + 15 + 130 = 150$.

steps.title: The share of the ₹5 coins
steps.body: Divide the money in ₹5 coins by the total money. The answer is option (C).

shortcut.body: Put $k = 1$: money is $5, 15, 130$, total 150, and $15/150 = 10\%$. About 30 seconds. The value-weighted step cannot be skipped; the count ratio alone gives a wrong share.

traps.text: Choosing 21%, the sum of the ratio parts, $5 + 3 + 13 = 21$, which is a count of parts and not a percentage.
Choosing $14\tfrac27\%$, which is $3/21$: the share of the number of coins that are ₹5. The question asks for the share of the money, and each ₹5 coin is worth five times a ₹1 coin.
Choosing 30% by mixing up the denominations, for example $3 \times 10 = 30$, and reading that number as a percentage. The ₹5 coins are worth $3 \times 5 = 15$ out of 150.

recognize.clues: A ratio of counts is given for items of different value, and the question asks for a percentage of money. That mismatch of units signals a value-weighted ratio.
recognize.contrast: A plain ratio question would ask for a share of the number of coins, which is $3/21$. Here each coin carries a different value, so the share of money is different from the share of coins.

check.body: Redo it with a different multiplier, $k = 2$, so the counts are 10, 6 and 26. The money is then 10, 30 and 260, total 300, and the ₹5 share must come out the same as before.

questions.stem: For positive non-zero real variables $p$ and $q$, if $\log(p^2 + q^2) = \log p + \log q + 2\log 3$, then, the value of $\frac{p^4 + q^4}{p^2 q^2}$ is

steps.title: The logarithm rules
steps.body: A sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product, $\log a + \log b = \log(ab)$, and a multiple of a logarithm is the logarithm of a power, $k\log a = \log(a^k)$. The logarithm is one-to-one for positive numbers, so $\log A = \log B$ means $A = B$. We use these to turn the given equation into an ordinary equation in $p$ and $q$.

steps.title: Turn the equation into algebra
steps.body: On the right, $2\log 3 = \log 9$, so the right side is $\log(9pq)$. Equal logarithms have equal insides.

steps.title: Rewrite the target using that equation
steps.body: Use $p^4 + q^4 = (p^2 + q^2)^2 - 2p^2q^2$, which is the identity $a^2 + b^2 = (a+b)^2 - 2ab$ with $a = p^2$, $b = q^2$. Divide by $p^2q^2$ and put in $p^2 + q^2 = 9pq$.

steps.title: Check that such numbers exist
steps.body: The equation $p^2 + q^2 = 9pq$ has positive solutions: with $u = p/q$ it is $u + 1/u = 9$, so $u = (9 + \sqrt{77})/2$ and a numerical check gives exactly 79 for the target. The answer is option (A).

shortcut.body: From the logs, $(p^2+q^2)/(pq) = 9$. The target is the square of that minus 2, so $9^2 - 2 = 79$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 81, which stops at $(p^2+q^2)^2/(p^2q^2)$ and forgets that $p^4 + q^4$ is that square minus $2p^2q^2$.
Choosing 9, which is the ratio $(p^2+q^2)/(pq)$ itself. The question asks for the fourth-power expression $(p^4+q^4)/(p^2q^2)$.
Choosing 83 by adding $2p^2q^2$ instead of subtracting it. Expanding $(p^2+q^2)^2 = p^4 + 2p^2q^2 + q^4$ shows the cross term has to come off.

recognize.clues: A sum of logarithms equals the logarithm of another expression, with a multiple $2\log 3$ in the tail. These ask for the product and power rules to get one equation.
recognize.contrast: A condition such as $\log(p^2+q^2) = \log p + \log q$ plus a constant is not a system to solve for $p$ and $q$ separately. Only the combination in the target is needed.

check.body: Solve for actual numbers. With $u = p/q$ the condition is $u + 1/u = 9$. Take the positive root, evaluate $u^2 + 1/u^2$ numerically, and compare it with the found value.

questions.stem:
A rectangular paper sheet of dimensions 54 cm × 4 cm is taken. The two longer edges of the sheet are joined together to create a cylindrical tube. A cube whose surface area is equal to the area of the sheet is also taken.

Then, the ratio of the volume of the cylindrical tube to the volume of the cube is

solutionDiagram.alt: A 54 by 4 sheet rolled along its long edges into a tube of height 54 and circumference 4 with radius 2 over pi and volume 216 over pi, beside a cube of side 6 and volume 216, giving ratio 1 over pi

steps.title: Rolling a sheet into a tube, and the two solids
steps.body: When you roll a rectangle and join two opposite edges, the joined edges form the seam and run along the length of the tube, so the seam length is the height $h$. The other side wraps once around and becomes the circumference of the circular end, $2\pi r$. A cylinder has volume $\pi r^2 h$. A cube of side $a$ has surface area $6a^2$ (six square faces) and volume $a^3$. The sheet is flat paper with no waste, so the cube's surface area equals the sheet's area, $54 \times 4$.

steps.title: The tube
steps.body: The longer edges (54 cm) are joined, so the seam is 54 cm: $h = 54$. The wrap-around side is 4 cm, so $2\pi r = 4$ and $r = 2/\pi$.

steps.title: The cube
steps.body: The sheet has area $54 \times 4 = 216$ cm$^2$. Setting $6a^2 = 216$ gives $a^2 = 36$, so $a = 6$ and the volume is $a^3 = 216$ cm$^3$.

steps.title: The ratio
steps.body: Divide the two volumes. The answer is option (A).

shortcut.body: A tube of circumference $C$ and height $h$ has $V = C^2h/(4\pi)$, because $r = C/(2\pi)$. With $C = 4$, $h = 54$: $16 \times 54/(4\pi) = 216/\pi$. The cube has $6a^2 = 216$, so $a = 6$ and $V = 216$. The ratio is $1/\pi$. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing $2/\pi$. This is a distractor: no single slip gives it. It would need a tube volume of $432/\pi$ against the cube's 216, and the true tube volume is $216/\pi$.
Choosing $3/\pi$. This is a distractor in the same family as $2/\pi$: no single slip gives it. It would need a tube volume of $648/\pi$, three times the true $216/\pi$.
Choosing $4/\pi$, which comes from $r = 4/\pi$, using the circumference as $\pi r$ instead of $2\pi r$. That makes the tube volume $864/\pi$.
Joining the short edges instead, so $h = 4$ and the circumference is 54. The ratio then is $13.5/\pi$, which is in no option. The stem says the longer edges are joined.

recognize.clues: A flat sheet is rolled into a cylinder and compared with a cube that has the same surface area, and the question asks for a ratio of volumes. That points to the cylinder and cube formulas.
recognize.contrast: This is not a plain geometry question about angles or lengths in a figure. The wording "longer edges are joined" decides which side is the height; joining the shorter edges would give a different tube.

check.body: A second route uses the tube's side area. The curved surface of the tube is the whole sheet, $2\pi r h = 4 \times 54 = 216$ with $r = 2/\pi$, so the radius is consistent. A cylinder's volume is half its radius times its curved area, giving $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{2}{\pi} \cdot 216 = 216/\pi$.

questions.stem:
The pie chart presents the percentage contribution of different macronutrients to a typical 2,000 kcal diet of a person.

The typical energy density (kcal/g) of these macronutrients is given in the table.

The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is
questions.figure: One pie chart titled "Macronutrient energy contribution", showing shares of the 2,000 kcal diet: Carbohydrates 35%, Proteins 20%, Unsaturated fat 20%, Saturated fat 20%, Trans fat 5%. The five shares add to 100%.

diagram.alt: Pie chart of a 2000 kcal diet: carbohydrates 35, proteins 20, unsaturated fat 20, saturated fat 20, trans fat 5 percent, beside a table of energy densities 4, 4, 9, 9, 9 kcal per gram

solutionDiagram.alt: A bar split into the five shares, with the three fat shares 20 plus 20 plus 5 equal to 45 percent of 2000 kcal, which is 900 kcal, and 900 divided by 9 kcal per gram equal to 100 grams

steps.title: Energy share versus mass
steps.body: A pie sector shows a share of the whole, here a share of the 2,000 kcal of energy, not a share of the weight. Energy density says how many kcal one gram holds, so $\text{grams} = \text{kcal} / \text{energy density}$. The question asks for grams of fat, so first find the energy that comes from fat, then divide by the density of fat. Carbohydrates and proteins are not asked for.

steps.title: Add the three fat sectors
steps.body: The fat sectors are unsaturated 20%, saturated 20% and trans 5%. As a check, all five sectors give $35 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 5 = 100$.

steps.title: Energy from fat
steps.body: Take 45% of the whole 2,000 kcal.

steps.title: Convert energy to grams
steps.body: All three fats have the same density, 9 kcal/g, so the total mass is the energy divided by 9. The answer is option (C).

shortcut.body: 45% of 2000 is 900, and $900 / 9 = 100$. About 45 seconds. Because all three fats share one density, the three sectors can be added before converting; with different densities each would be converted separately.

traps.text: Choosing 44.4, which is $400/9$: only one fat sector (20% of 2,000 kcal). The question asks for all three fat types.
Choosing 77.8, which is $700/9$: it uses the 35% carbohydrate sector, not the fat sectors.
Choosing 3,600, which is $900 \times 4$: multiplying the fat energy by the carbohydrate density. Grams come from dividing kcal by kcal per gram, and fat uses 9.

recognize.clues: A pie chart gives percentage shares of a 2,000 kcal total, a table gives kcal per gram, and the question asks for a mass covering several slices together. The chart and the table must be read together.
recognize.contrast: It looks like a plain percentages question, but the share is of energy and the answer is a mass, so a conversion through the density is needed at the end.

check.body: Add up the other side. The non-fat slices are $35 + 20 = 55\%$ of 2,000 kcal, which is 1,100 kcal, and 1,100 plus the fat energy must make 2,000. Going back from the mass, 100 g of fat at 9 kcal/g is 900 kcal, which is 45% of 2,000.

questions.stem:
A series of natural numbers $F_1, F_2, F_3, F_4, F_5, F_6, F_7, \dots$ obeys $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$ for all integers $n \ge 2$.

If $F_6 = 37$, and $F_7 = 60$, then what is $F_1$?

steps.title: The recurrence and how to run it backwards
steps.body: A recurrence is a rule that builds each term from earlier ones. Here every term after the second is the sum of the two terms before it, so $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$. The rule can be turned around: a term equals the term two places ahead minus the term one place ahead, that is $F_{n-1} = F_{n+1} - F_n$. The rule holds for $n \ge 2$, so it applies all the way down to $F_3 = F_2 + F_1$. Given the last two terms, subtract repeatedly to walk back to $F_1$.

steps.title: Check forward
steps.body: Starting from $4, 5$ and adding the last two each time gives $4, 5, 9, 14, 23, 37, 60$, which ends at $F_6 = 37$ and $F_7 = 60$ and has only natural numbers. So $F_1 = 4$, option (A).

shortcut.body: Write the terms through $F_1, F_2$: $F_6 = 3F_1 + 5F_2 = 37$ and $F_7 = 5F_1 + 8F_2 = 60$. Test the options in the first equation, then confirm with the second: $F_1 = 4$ gives $F_2 = 5$ and $F_7 = 20 + 40 = 60$. Or subtract backward five times, about 40 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 5, which is $F_2$. The backward walk was stopped one step too early.
Choosing 8, which fits neither equation: $F_1 = 8$ makes $F_2 = 13/5$ in $3F_1 + 5F_2 = 37$, not even a natural number. It is a subtraction slip in the backward chain.
Choosing 9, which is $F_3$ (the walk stopped two steps early) and is a trap in another way: $F_1 = 9, F_2 = 2$ satisfies $F_6 = 37$ but gives $F_7 = 61$, not 60. Both given terms must be checked.

recognize.clues: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it, the last two terms are given, and the first term is asked. That is a recurrence to be run backwards.
recognize.contrast: It is not an arithmetic or a geometric progression, since there is no common difference or ratio. The rule uses two earlier terms, so you step back by subtraction rather than apply a closed formula.

check.body: Here is a route with no backward chain. Write $F_7 = 5F_1 + 8F_2 = 60$. Then $8F_2$ is a multiple of 5 that is at most 60, so $F_2 = 5$ (the next choice, 10, gives 80). That gives $F_1 = (60 - 40)/5 = 4$, and $3F_1 + 5F_2 = 12 + 25 = 37$ agrees with $F_6$.

questions.stem:
Consider two functions of time $(t)$,

$f(t) = 0.01\, t^2$

$g(t) = 4\, t$

where $0 < t < \infty$.

Now consider the following two statements:

(i) For some $t > 0$, $g(t) > f(t)$.

(ii) There exists a $T$, such that $f(t) > g(t)$ for all $t > T$.

Which one of the following options is TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: Plot of g(t) = 4t as a dashed line and f(t) = 0.01 t squared as a solid parabola; g is above f for t below 400, they meet at t = 400 where both equal 1600, and f is above g after that

steps.title: The two kinds of claim
steps.body: "For some $t$" is satisfied by a single value of $t$ where the inequality holds. "There exists a $T$ such that for all $t > T$" says that from some point on the inequality holds at every $t$ and never fails again. To test both, find exactly where the two functions cross. A quadratic $t^2$ eventually outgrows a straight line $t$, whatever the coefficients, because the ratio $f/g$ grows without bound.

steps.title: Find where $f > g$
steps.body: For $t > 0$ we may divide by $t$ without flipping the inequality. Then $f(t) > g(t)$ means $0.01t^2 > 4t$, that is $0.01t > 4$.

steps.title: Test statement (i)
steps.body: By step 2, $g(t) > f(t)$ for $0 < t < 400$. For example, at $t = 100$ we get $g = 400$ and $f = 0.01 \times 10000 = 100$, so $g > f$. Statement (i) is true.

steps.title: Test statement (ii)
steps.body: Take $T = 400$. For every $t > 400$, step 2 gives $f(t) > g(t)$; for example at $t = 500$, $f = 2500$ and $g = 2000$. Statement (ii) is true. Both statements are true, option (C).

shortcut.body: The ratio $f/g = t/400$. It is below 1 for small $t$ (so $g$ wins somewhere, (i) true) and above 1 for every $t > 400$ (so $f$ wins for good, (ii) true). Both, option (C), in about 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing "only (i)", by thinking the bigger coefficient 4 keeps $g$ ahead for ever. A quadratic eventually beats any line, here from $t = 400$.
Choosing "only (ii)", by thinking that because $f$ wins in the end it wins everywhere. For $0 < t < 400$ the line is above the parabola, so (i) is also true; it needs just one such $t$.
Choosing "neither", which reads (i) as "always" and (ii) as "never". Statement (i) asks only for some $t$, and (ii) holds from $T = 400$ on.

recognize.clues: A quadratic is compared with a straight line, and the statements are about some small $t$ and about all large $t$. The growth of $t^2$ against $t$ decides the second statement.
recognize.contrast: Both functions are polynomials, so the one of higher degree wins in the end whatever the coefficients. The coefficients only decide where the crossing is, and that tells apart "for some $t$" from "for all large $t$".

check.body: Test points on both sides of the crossing and at it. At $t = 400$ both functions equal 1600. At $t = 1000$ the parabola gives 10000 against 4000, and at $t = 10$ it gives 1 against 40, so each ordering really occurs.

questions.stem:
A function $y(x)$ is defined in the interval $[0, 1]$ on the $x$-axis as

$y(x) = 2$ if $0 \le x < \frac{1}{3}$

$y(x) = 3$ if $\frac{1}{3} \le x < \frac{3}{4}$

$y(x) = 1$ if $\frac{3}{4} \le x \le 1$

Which one of the following is the area under the curve for the interval $[0, 1]$ on the $x$-axis?

solutionDiagram.alt: Step function y(x) on [0,1]: three rectangles of heights 2, 3 and 1 over widths 1/3, 5/12 and 1/4 with areas 2/3, 5/4 and 1/4, adding to 13/6

steps.title: What area under a curve means here
steps.body: The curve $y(x)$ gives a height above each point of the $x$-axis. The area under the curve is the area of the region between the curve and the $x$-axis. This function is flat on each of three intervals, and over a flat piece the region is a rectangle, so its area is height times width, where width is the right end minus the left end. A single point has no width, so it does not matter whether an end point belongs to one piece or the next. The area over $[0,1]$ is the sum of the three rectangle areas.

steps.title: Find the width of each piece
steps.body: First piece: from $0$ to $\frac13$, width $\frac13 = \frac{4}{12}$. Second piece: from $\frac13$ to $\frac34$, width $\frac34 - \frac13 = \frac{9}{12} - \frac{4}{12} = \frac{5}{12}$. Third piece: from $\frac34$ to $1$, width $\frac14 = \frac{3}{12}$. The widths add to $\frac{4+5+3}{12} = 1$, which is the length of $[0,1]$, so no part of the interval is missed or counted twice.

steps.title: Multiply and add
steps.body: Heights are $2$, $3$ and $1$. Areas: $2 \times \frac13 = \frac23$, then $3 \times \frac{5}{12} = \frac{15}{12} = \frac54$, then $1 \times \frac14 = \frac14$. Put everything over $12$ and add. The total is $\frac{26}{12} = \frac{13}{6}$, which is option (C). The drawing shows the three rectangles with their areas.

shortcut.body: Every height is at least $1$ and the base has length $1$, so the area is at least $1$. That removes (A) and (D). The first two rectangles alone already give $\frac23 + \frac54 = \frac{23}{12} \approx 1.92$, which is more than $\frac65$, so (B) goes too. Only $\frac{13}{6}$ is left, and a one-line sum over $12$ confirms it. About 1 minute.

Choosing $\frac65$. It clears the lower bound of $1$, but the first two rectangles alone already add up to $\frac{23}{12}$, which is more than $\frac65$. Passing the lower bound is not enough; the sum has to be checked.
Choosing $\frac{6}{13}$. This is the reciprocal of the correct area and is below $1$, so it cannot be an area under a curve whose height is at least $1$ everywhere.

questions.stem:
Let $r$ be a root of the equation $x^2 + 2x + 6 = 0$.

Then the value of the expression $(r+2)(r+3)(r+4)(r+5)$ is

steps.title: What a root gives us
steps.body: A root of an equation is a number that makes it true when substituted. So $r$ satisfies $r^2 + 2r + 6 = 0$. Here the discriminant is $2^2 - 4\cdot 6 = -20 < 0$, so $r$ is not a real number, and we never need its value. The one fact we use is the equation itself. The method: rewrite the expression so that the equation can replace a whole block of it, instead of finding $r$.

steps.title: Complete the square
steps.body: Add and subtract $1$ so that $r^2 + 2r$ becomes a perfect square: $r^2 + 2r + 6 = (r+1)^2 + 5$. Since this equals $0$, we get $(r+1)^2 = -5$. Write $t = r + 1$, so that $t^2 = -5$. The four factors become $t+1$, $t+2$, $t+3$, $t+4$, because $r+2 = t+1$ and so on.

steps.title: Pair the factors so the middle terms match
steps.body: Multiply the outer pair and the inner pair: $(t+1)(t+4) = t^2 + 5t + 4$ and $(t+2)(t+3) = t^2 + 5t + 6$. Put $t^2 = -5$ in both: the first becomes $5t - 1$ and the second becomes $5t + 1$. These two differ only in the sign of the constant, so their product is a difference of squares.

steps.title: Multiply and read the option
steps.body: $(5t-1)(5t+1) = 25t^2 - 1 = 25(-5) - 1 = -126$. That is option (D). As a check, take the root $r = -1 + i\sqrt5$: then $(r+2)(r+3)(r+4)(r+5)$ evaluates to $-126$ with no imaginary part, and the other root gives the same value.

shortcut.body: Complete the square at once: $(r+1)^2 = -5$. The four factors are $(t+1)(t+2)(t+3)(t+4)$ with $t = r+1$. Pair $(t+1)(t+4)$ and $(t+2)(t+3)$ to get $(5t-1)(5t+1) = 25t^2 - 1 = -126$. Do not try to find $r$: it is complex. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing $51$. It is the mirror of option (B) with the sign lost. The roots are not real, so $(r+1)^2$ is negative and the final product must be negative.
Choosing $-51$. It has the right sign but the wrong magnitude, and it matches no consistent reading of the equation. The constant is $6$, so $(r+1)^2 = 1 - 6 = -5$ and $25(-5) - 1 = -126$.
Choosing $126$. This is the right size with the sign dropped. A real $r$ would give a positive square, but $(r+1)^2 = -5$ is negative, so $25t^2 - 1$ is $-126$, not $+126$.

recognize.clues: The expression is a product of four consecutive shifts of a root of a quadratic that has no real roots. Powers of the root can be traded using the equation.
recognize.contrast: This is not a solve-for-$r$ question. The roots are complex, so you use the relation the root obeys instead of computing $r$.

check.body: Pair the factors the other way round, without shifting. $(r+2)(r+5) = r^2 + 7r + 10$ and $(r+3)(r+4) = r^2 + 7r + 12$. Using $r^2 = -2r - 6$ these become $5r + 4$ and $5r + 6$, and their product is $25r^2 + 50r + 24 = 25(r^2 + 2r) + 24 = 25(-6) + 24$.
