questions.stem:
A box contains five balls of same size and shape. Three of them are green coloured balls and two of them are orange coloured balls. Balls are drawn from the box one at a time. If a green ball is drawn, it is not replaced. If an orange ball is drawn, it is replaced with another orange ball.

First ball is drawn. What is the probability of getting an orange ball in the next draw?

solutionDiagram.alt: Probability tree: first draw green with 3/5 then orange with 2/4 gives 3/10; first draw orange with 2/5 then orange with 2/5 gives 4/25; the two add to 23/50

steps.title: Probability with a first draw that changes the box
steps.body: Probability of an event is the number of favourable balls divided by the number of balls in the box, when every ball is equally likely to be drawn. Here the box after the first draw depends on what the first draw was, so we split into cases by the first draw. The rule is the law of total probability: $P(\text{orange next}) = \sum P(\text{first draw}) \times P(\text{orange next} \mid \text{first draw})$, where the vertical bar means 'given that'. The cases are exhaustive (green or orange) and cannot happen together, so their contributions add.

steps.title: Case 1: the first ball is green
steps.body: The first draw is green with probability $\frac35$. A green ball is not put back, so the box now has $2$ green and $2$ orange balls, $4$ in all. The chance the next ball is orange is $\frac24 = \frac12$. This case contributes $\frac35 \times \frac12 = \frac{3}{10}$.

steps.title: Case 2: the first ball is orange
steps.body: The first draw is orange with probability $\frac25$. The orange ball is replaced by another orange ball, so the box is unchanged: $3$ green and $2$ orange. The chance the next ball is orange is $\frac25$. This case contributes $\frac25 \times \frac25 = \frac{4}{25}$.

steps.title: Add the cases
steps.body: $\frac{3}{10} + \frac{4}{25} = \frac{15}{50} + \frac{8}{50} = \frac{23}{50} = 0.46$. This matches option (D). The tree in the drawing shows the two branches and their products.

shortcut.body: Draw a two-branch tree and read the products: green first gives $0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.30$, orange first gives $0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16$, and the sum is $0.46 = \frac{23}{50}$. In decimals the options are $0.5$, $0.32$, $0.38$ and $0.46$, so the sum picks (D) at once. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing $\frac12$. It is what you get if an orange draw is treated as adding a ball without taking one out (box of $6$ with $3$ orange, chance $\frac36$): then $\frac{3}{10} + \frac25\cdot\frac12 = \frac12$. The orange ball is replaced, so the box stays at $5$ balls.
Choosing $\frac{8}{25}$. This is $2 \times \frac{4}{25}$: the orange-then-orange branch counted twice and the green branch left out. Both branches must be counted once.

Choosing $\frac{19}{50}$. This is $\frac{3}{10} + \frac{2}{25}$, which uses $\frac15$ for the orange-first branch instead of $\frac25$. After the orange is swapped for another orange there are still $2$ orange balls in $5$.

recognize.clues: The box changes depending on the colour of the first ball, and the question asks about the second draw without telling the first. That calls for splitting on the first draw.
recognize.contrast: It is not a Bayes reversal, where the later outcome is known and the earlier one is asked. Here we move forward, and the draws are not independent because the replacement rule depends on the colour.

check.body: Find the chance of a green ball next with the same tree and see whether the two add to 1. Green then green is $\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac24 = \tfrac3{10}$ and orange then green is $\tfrac25\cdot\tfrac35 = \tfrac6{25}$, so green next is $\tfrac{27}{50}$. Then $\tfrac{23}{50} + \tfrac{27}{50} = 1$.

questions.stem:
The corners and mid-points of the sides of a triangle are named using the distinct letters P, Q, R, S, T and U, but not necessarily in the same order. Consider the following statements:

The line joining P and R is parallel to the line joining Q and S.

P is placed on the side opposite to the corner T.

S and U cannot be placed on the same side.

Which one of the following statements is correct based on the above information?

solutionDiagram.alt: Triangle ABC with mid-points D, E, F: if S sat at corner A then U is forced to D, but both mid-segments F-D and E-D that could be parallel to a side need D

options: P cannot be placed at a corner
S cannot be placed at a corner
U cannot be placed at a mid-point
R cannot be placed at a corner

steps.title: The six points and the one parallel fact
steps.body: A triangle has $3$ corners and $3$ mid-points (the point halfway along each side). Name the corners $A, B, C$ and the mid-points $D, E, F$ of $BC, CA, AB$. Every side carries three of the points: its two corners and its mid-point. 'On a side' includes its corners. The key fact is the mid-segment theorem: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides is parallel to the third side. Of the $15$ lines through two of the six points, $9$ run along the sides, $3$ are mid-segments $DE, EF, FD$, and $3$ are medians $AD, BE, CF$. A median is parallel to none of the others. So 'PR is parallel to QS' (four different points) means: one pair lies on a side and the other pair is the mid-segment parallel to that side.

steps.title: Suppose S is a corner and see what is forced
steps.body: Take $S = A$ (the other corners work the same way). The third statement says $U$ shares no side with $S$. The sides through $A$ hold $B, F, C, E$, so $U$ must be the only point left, $D$, the mid-point of the side opposite $A$. Now the line $QS$ passes through $A$ and through $Q \ne U$, so $Q$ is not $D$. Then line $AQ$ lies along a side: $AB$ or $AC$. Its parallel partner $PR$ has to be the mid-segment parallel to that side: $ED$ (parallel to $AB$) or $FD$ (parallel to $AC$).

steps.title: The contradiction
steps.body: Both mid-segments contain $D$, but $D$ is $U$, and $P$ and $R$ are different letters from $U$. So no choice of $P$ and $R$ fits. Therefore $S$ can never be placed at a corner, which is option (B). The drawing shows $S = A$, the forced $U = D$, and the two dashed mid-segments that both end at $D$.

steps.title: Why the other three statements are false
steps.body: Show one arrangement that satisfies all three conditions: $P = A$, $Q = D$, $R = B$, $S = E$, $T = C$, $U = F$. Check: $PR = AB$ and $QS = DE$ are parallel (mid-segment theorem). $P = A$ lies on $AB$, the side opposite $T = C$. $S = E$ lies only on side $CA$ and $U = F$ only on $AB$, so they share no side. In it $P$ is at a corner, which kills (A). $U$ is at a mid-point, which kills (C). $R$ is at a corner, which kills (D). A script that tries all $720$ namings finds $30$ valid ones, and in none of them is $S$ at a corner.

shortcut.body: Build one valid arrangement and see that it breaks (A), (C) and (D) together: $P = A$, $R = B$ on side $AB$, $T = C$ opposite, then $Q, S$ as the mid-segment $D, E$ parallel to $AB$, leaving $U = F$. Only (B) survives. This works because exactly one option is correct. Without that guarantee you would need the forcing argument. About 3 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 'P cannot be placed at a corner'. The clue says only that $P$ is on the side opposite $T$, and a corner of that side counts as being on it. $P = A$ with $T = C$ is allowed. Reading 'on the side' as 'at the middle of the side' would wrongly force $P$ to a mid-point.
Choosing 'U cannot be placed at a mid-point'. In the arrangement above $U = F$, a mid-point, and every condition holds.
Choosing 'R cannot be placed at a corner'. Parallel lines may end at corners: $PR = AB$ has $R = B$ at a corner.

recognize.clues: Six letters go on the three corners and three mid-points of a triangle, with one clue about parallel lines and one about sharing a side. The mid-segment fact about triangles is the tool.
recognize.contrast: It looks like a counting problem over all namings of the six points, but the parallel clue forces the structure, so a few geometric facts replace the count.

check.body: Go through every partner Q for S = A, with U forced to D. Q = B or F puts line QS along side AB, so PR must be the mid-segment ED. Q = C or E puts it along side AC, so PR must be FD. Q = D is excluded because U is already D, and the median through D is parallel to nothing anyway. Each of the four live cases needs D inside PR, which is impossible when D is U. A direct count of all 720 namings gives 30 valid ones, with S at a mid-point in every one.

questions.stem: If $\theta$ is the angle, in degrees, between the longest diagonal of the cube and any one of the edges of the cube, then, $\cos\theta =$

solutionDiagram.alt: Unit cube with edge OP, long diagonal OG and face diagonal PG forming a right triangle at P with sides 1, root 2 and root 3, so cos theta is 1 over root 3

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A cube has $12$ equal edges and $6$ square faces. A face diagonal joins opposite corners of one face. The longest diagonal (the space diagonal) joins opposite corners of the whole cube, passing through the centre. The angle between two lines that meet at a point is measured at that point. We use a right triangle: for an acute angle $\theta$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent side}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, and the Pythagoras rule $\text{hyp}^2 = \text{leg}_1^2 + \text{leg}_2^2$ finds lengths.

steps.title: Build a right triangle inside the cube
steps.body: Let the cube have side $1$. Start at a corner $O$. Take the edge $OP$ from $O$, and the space diagonal $OG$ from $O$ to the opposite corner $G$. The segment $PG$ lies in the face that contains $P$ and $G$, and it is perpendicular to the edge $OP$, because $OP$ is perpendicular to that whole face. So triangle $OPG$ has a right angle at $P$, and $\theta$ is the angle at $O$.

steps.title: Lengths and the cosine
steps.body: $OP = 1$, an edge. $PG$ is a diagonal of a unit square, so $PG = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2$. Then $OG^2 = OP^2 + PG^2 = 1 + 2 = 3$, so $OG = \sqrt3$. The side next to $\theta$ is $OP = 1$ and the hypotenuse is $OG = \sqrt3$. Hence $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.577$, about $54.7^\circ$. This is option (B). An edge that does not touch the diagonal is parallel to one that does, so it makes the same angle, and by symmetry every edge at $O$ gives this triangle again.

shortcut.body: Put the cube in coordinates: the long diagonal is the vector $(1,1,1)$ and an edge is $(1,0,0)$. Dot product over lengths: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3\cdot 1}$. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $\frac12$, which is $\cos 60^\circ$. It comes from assuming an equilateral or $30$-$60$-$90$ picture. The triangle $OPG$ has sides $1, \sqrt2, \sqrt3$, not $1, 2$ and $\sqrt3$.
Choosing $\frac1{\sqrt2}$, which is $\cos 45^\circ$. That is the angle between an edge and a face diagonal, not the long diagonal.
Choosing $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. It would make $\theta = 30^\circ$. It is the cosine of the smaller angle of a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle; here the ratio adjacent to hypotenuse is $1:\sqrt3$.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the angle between two lines of a solid, a long diagonal and an edge, and every option is a simple cosine value, which points to a right triangle inside the cube.
recognize.contrast: This is not a mensuration question about volume or area: no size is asked, only a ratio of lengths. The angle does not depend on the side length, so take the side as 1.

check.body: The cube is symmetric, so the long diagonal must make equal angles with the three edges at its corner. The squares of the three cosines must then add to 1, because the diagonal direction has unit length. Three equal values $c^2$ with $3c^2=1$ give the same value as the triangle.

questions.stem: If $\left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 - \left(x - \frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = x + 2$, then the value of $x$ is:

steps.title: The identity that removes the squares
steps.body: A difference of two squares factors as $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$: check by multiplying out, $(a-b)(a+b) = a^2 + ab - ab - b^2$. When two squared brackets are subtracted, this turns a quadratic-looking equation into a linear one, because the $x^2$ terms cancel.

steps.title: Apply it
steps.body: Let $a = x - \frac12$ and $b = x - \frac32$. Then $a - b = -\frac12 + \frac32 = 1$ and $a + b = 2x - 2$. So the left side is $1 \times (2x - 2) = 2x - 2$.

steps.title: Solve and check
steps.body: $2x - 2 = x + 2$ gives $x = 4$, option (B). Check: $\left(3.5\right)^2 - \left(2.5\right)^2 = 12.25 - 6.25 = 6$, and $x + 2 = 6$.

shortcut.body: Substitute the options into the right side and left side: $x=4$ gives $3.5^2 - 2.5^2 = 6$ and $4 + 2 = 6$. Only one option can work, so one check suffices. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $2$. This comes from forgetting the $-2$ in $a + b = 2x - 2$, which gives $2x = x + 2$. Check $x = 2$: $1.5^2 - 0.5^2 = 2$ but $x + 2 = 4$.
Choosing $6$. That is the value of the right side, $x + 2$ when $x = 4$, so it answers 'what is the value of both sides' rather than 'what is $x$'.
Choosing $8$. That is $2x$ for the correct $x$. Check $x = 8$: $7.5^2 - 6.5^2 = 14$ but $x + 2 = 10$.

recognize.clues: Two squared brackets of the same variable are subtracted, and the right side is only linear in $x$. That shape signals that the squares cancel and the algebra collapses.
recognize.contrast: This is not a quadratic to be solved by the formula: expanding each bracket separately wastes time and hides that the $x^2$ terms cancel.

check.body: Expand the squares instead of factoring: $(x^2 - x + \frac14) - (x^2 - 3x + \frac94) = 2x - 2$, so the equation is $2x-2=x+2$ and $x=4$ again. A wrong option fails: $x=2$ gives $1.5^2-0.5^2=2$ but $x+2=4$.

The number of students in three classes is in the ratio 3:13:6. If 18 students are added to each class, the ratio changes to 15:35:21.

The total number of students in all the three classes in the beginning was:

steps.title: What a ratio says, and why adding breaks it
steps.body: A ratio $3:13:6$ means the class sizes are $3k$, $13k$ and $6k$ for one common positive number $k$. Two lists are in the ratio $15:35:21$ when each size divided by its ratio number gives the same value. Adding the same number $18$ to all three classes changes the ratio, because ratios compare sizes by multiplication, not addition. So the new sizes $3k+18$, $13k+18$, $6k+18$ must be $15m$, $35m$, $21m$ for some common $m$.

steps.title: Equate two of the quotients
steps.body: From the first two classes: $\dfrac{3k+18}{15} = \dfrac{13k+18}{35}$. Cross-multiply: $35(3k+18) = 15(13k+18)$, so $105k + 630 = 195k + 270$, so $360 = 90k$ and $k = 4$.

steps.title: Check with the third class and find the total
steps.body: For $k = 4$ the new sizes are $30, 70, 42$. Divided by $15, 35, 21$ they give $2, 2, 2$, so the new ratio is right (all three quotients are equal). The original sizes are $12, 52, 24$, with total $88$. Equivalently the total is $(3+13+6)k = 22 \times 4 = 88$. This is option (C).

shortcut.body: The total is $22k$, so each option fixes $k$: $1, 3, 4, 5$. The first class after adding is $3k+18$ and must be a multiple of $15$: $21, 27, 30, 33$. Only $k = 4$ gives $30$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $22$. This is only the sum of the ratio numbers, $k = 1$. Then the first class would be $3 + 18 = 21$, not a multiple of $15$.
Choosing $66$ ($k = 3$). The new sizes would be $27, 57, 36$, which are not in the ratio $15:35:21$.
Choosing $110$ ($k = 5$). The new sizes would be $33, 83, 48$, which are not in the ratio $15:35:21$. Another slip is adding $18$ directly to the ratio numbers, which is meaningless.

recognize.clues: Three quantities are given as a ratio, then the same amount is added to each, and a new ratio is given. Two ratios before and after link to one unknown multiplier.
recognize.contrast: This differs from a plain ratio split: the added amount is not proportional, so you cannot just scale the new ratio back. Use the multiplier on the old sizes and add 18 to each.

check.body: Instead of solving, test each option against the third class. The total fixes $k$ for each option, and the third class after adding must be a multiple of $21$. Only one option gives a multiple of $21$.

questions.stem:
The number of units of a product sold in three different years and the respective net profits are presented in the figure above. The cost/unit in Year 3 was Rs. 1, which was half the cost/unit in Year 2. The cost/unit in Year 3 was one-third of the cost/unit in Year 1. Taxes were paid on the selling price at 10%, 13% and 15% respectively for the three years. Net profit is calculated as the difference between the selling price and the sum of cost and taxes paid in that year.

The ratio of the selling price in Year 2 to the selling price in Year 3 is ______.
questions.figure: Bar chart with two bars for each of Year 1, Year 2 and Year 3. Number of units (hatched bars): Year 1 = 100, Year 2 = 200, Year 3 = 300. Net profit in Rs. (solid bars): Year 1 = 240, Year 2 = 296, Year 3 = 210. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 350.

diagram.alt: Grouped bar chart: units sold are 100, 200, 300 and net profit is 240, 296, 210 in Years 1, 2 and 3

steps.title: The terms and the one equation
steps.body: Selling price (SP) is the total money received from selling all the units in a year. Cost is the cost per unit times the number of units. Tax is a percentage of the selling price. The question defines net profit as SP minus (cost plus tax). With tax rate $t$, that is $\text{NP} = \text{SP} - \text{cost} - t\cdot\text{SP} = (1-t)\,\text{SP} - \text{cost}$. Solving for the unknown selling price gives the rule used below.

steps.title: Read the chart and find each year's total cost
steps.body: Units sold: $100$, $200$, $300$. Net profit: $240$, $296$, $210$. The cost per unit in Year 3 is Rs. 1, and it is half of Year 2's, so Year 2's is Rs. 2 per unit. Year 1's cost per unit ($3$) is not needed. Total cost, Year 3: $1 \times 300 = 300$. Total cost, Year 2: $2 \times 200 = 400$.

steps.title: Selling price of Year 3 and Year 2
Ratio and check
steps.body: $\text{SP}_2 : \text{SP}_3 = 800 : 600 = 4 : 3$, option (A). Check Year 2: tax $= 0.13 \times 800 = 104$ and $800 - 400 - 104 = 296$. Check Year 3: tax $= 0.15 \times 600 = 90$ and $600 - 300 - 90 = 210$. Both match the chart.

shortcut.body: Only Years 2 and 3 matter; Year 1 is a distraction. The numbers are built to divide cleanly: $87 \times 8 = 696$ and $85 \times 6 = 510$. So $\text{SP}_2 = 800$ and $\text{SP}_3 = 600$, ratio $4:3$. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing $1:1$. Nothing in the data makes the two selling prices equal. Using the formula gives $800$ and $600$. It is a guess from the similar net profits $296$ and $210$ plus cost, without dividing by $1-t$.
Choosing $3:4$. This is the ratio Year 3 to Year 2, the question asks Year 2 to Year 3.

Choosing $1:2$. This is the inverse of the ratio of per-unit selling prices ($800/200 = 4$ against $600/300 = 2$, which is $2:1$). It also equals the ratio of the Year 1 units to Year 2 units ($100:200$) read from the wrong bars. The question asks for total selling prices.

recognize.clues: Values come from a chart (units and net profit), with extra facts in words about cost per unit and tax rates. The ratio of two derived quantities is asked, not a value read straight off the chart.
recognize.contrast: This is not a plain percentage question on one number: tax is on the selling price while cost is per unit, so each year needs its own total cost and its own rate.

check.body: Look at each year as fractions of its selling price. Year 2: cost $400$ is $50\%$ of $800$ and tax is $13\%$, leaving $37\%$, and $296 \div 800 = 0.37$. Year 3: cost $300$ is $50\%$ of $600$ and tax is $15\%$, leaving $35\%$, and $210 \div 600 = 0.35$. Both agree with the chart.

questions.stem:
The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 7 to 3.

Among the options below, an acceptable value for the total number of students in the class is:

steps.title: What the ratio forces
steps.body: A ratio $7:3$ means that for every $7$ boys there are $3$ girls, so the class is made of equal groups of $7 + 3 = 10$ students. If there are $k$ groups, there are $7k$ boys and $3k$ girls. Students come in whole numbers, so $k$ must be a whole number (strictly, boys $= \frac{7}{10}N$ and girls $= \frac{3}{10}N$ must both be whole). The rule: the total $N$ must be a multiple of $10$.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: $21$: boys $14.7$, girls $6.3$, not whole. $37$: boys $25.9$, girls $11.1$, no. $73$: boys $51.1$, girls $21.9$, no. $50$: boys $\frac{7}{10}\times 50 = 35$, girls $\frac{3}{10}\times 50 = 15$, both whole. So the answer is option (C), $50$.

shortcut.body: The total must be a multiple of $7 + 3 = 10$. Only $50$ ends in $0$. About 5 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $21$. It is $7 \times 3$, the product of the ratio numbers. The groups are formed by the sum $7+3$, not the product.
Choosing $37$. It reuses the digits $3$ and $7$ of the ratio but is not a multiple of $10$, so the boys and girls would not be whole numbers ($25.9$ and $11.1$).
Choosing $73$. It also reuses the digits of the ratio and is not a multiple of $10$ ($51.1$ boys and $21.9$ girls).

recognize.clues: A ratio of two counts of people is given, and the question asks which total is possible. Counts of people must be whole numbers.
recognize.contrast: This is not a ratio-splitting question with a given total: here the total is unknown and the ratio restricts which totals are possible.

check.body: For $50$: boys $35$, girls $15$, and $35:15 = 7:3$. For a rejected option, $21$: boys $14.7$ and girls $6.3$. Since $7$ and $10$ share no factor, $\frac{7N}{10}$ is whole only when $10 \mid N$, which only $50$ satisfies.

questions.stem: We have 2 rectangular sheets of paper, M and N, of dimensions 6 cm $\times$ 1 cm each. Sheet M is rolled to form an open cylinder by bringing the short edges of the sheet together. Sheet N is cut into equal square patches and assembled to form the largest possible closed cube. Assuming the ends of the cylinder are closed, the ratio of the volume of the cylinder to that of the cube is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Sheet M rolled into a cylinder of radius 3 over pi and height 1 with volume 9 over pi, beside sheet N cut into six unit squares forming a cube of volume 1

steps.title: Terms and formulas
steps.body: Rolling a rectangle into a tube joins two opposite edges. The edge that is bent around becomes the circle at the end, so its length is the circumference $2\pi r$; the other side becomes the height $h$. Volume of a cylinder $= \pi r^2 h$. A cube of side $s$ has $6$ square faces of area $s^2$ each, and volume $s^3$. The ratio of two volumes is one divided by the other, and the unit cm$^3$ cancels.

steps.title: The cylinder from sheet M
steps.body: Bringing the short edges ($1$ cm) together means the long side of $6$ cm goes around the tube. So the circumference is $6$ and the height is $1$. From $2\pi r = 6$ we get $r = \frac{3}{\pi}$. The volume is $\pi \left(\frac{3}{\pi}\right)^2 \times 1 = \frac{9}{\pi}$ cm$^3$, about $2.86$.

steps.title: The cube from sheet N
steps.body: Sheet N has area $6 \times 1 = 6$ cm$^2$. A closed cube needs $6$ faces, so each face can have area at most $6 \div 6 = 1$ cm$^2$, which means a side of at most $1$ cm. The strip cuts exactly into six $1 \times 1$ squares with nothing left over, so the largest cube has side $1$ and volume $1$ cm$^3$.

steps.title: The ratio
steps.body: $\dfrac{9/\pi}{1} = \dfrac{9}{\pi}$, option (C).

shortcut.body: Use the shortcut $V = \dfrac{C^2 h}{4\pi}$ for a cylinder with circumference $C$: $\dfrac{36 \times 1}{4\pi} = \dfrac{9}{\pi}$. For the cube, total area $6 = 6s^2$, so $s = 1$ and the volume is $1$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $\frac\pi2 \approx 1.57$. The cylinder here has volume near $2.86$ and the cube volume is $1$, so the ratio is near $2.86$. $\frac\pi2$ is too small.
Choosing $\frac3\pi$. That is the radius $r$, not a ratio of volumes. A volume needs $\pi r^2 h$, not $r$.
Choosing $3\pi \approx 9.42$. Taking $6$ as the diameter would give $r = 3$ and a volume of $9\pi$; either way $3\pi$ is far from the true ratio of about $2.86$.

recognize.clues: A flat sheet is turned into a cylinder and into a cube, and the ratio of the two volumes is asked. Sheet dimensions fix the circumference and the face area.
recognize.contrast: This is not a surface-area question: the area of the sheet only limits the cube, while the cylinder is set by which edges are joined.

check.body: Use the formula $V = \dfrac{C^2 h}{4\pi}$ for a tube with circumference $C$ and height $h$ (from $r = C/2\pi$). With $C=6$, $h=1$: $\dfrac{36}{4\pi} = \dfrac{9}{\pi}$, matching $\pi r^2 h$. Rolling the other way ($C=1$, $h=6$) gives $\dfrac{6}{4\pi}$, a different value, so the choice of edges matters. The six unit squares also tile the $6\times1$ strip exactly.

questions.stem:
Details of prices of two items P and Q are presented in the above table. The ratio of cost of item P to cost of item Q is 3:4. Discount is calculated as the difference between the marked price and the selling price. The profit percentage is calculated as the ratio of the difference between selling price and cost, to the cost $\left(\text{Profit \%} = \dfrac{\text{Selling price} - \text{Cost}}{\text{Cost}} \times 100\right)$.

The discount on item Q, as a percentage of its marked price, is ______

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: Cost is what the seller paid. Marked price (MP) is the price printed on the item. Selling price (SP) is what the buyer actually pays. Profit percent is measured on cost: $\text{SP} = \text{Cost}\left(1 + \frac{\text{profit}\%}{100}\right)$. Discount is $\text{MP} - \text{SP}$, and here it is asked as a percentage of the marked price, so the denominator is MP: $\text{discount}\% = \frac{\text{MP} - \text{SP}}{\text{MP}} \times 100$. Two different bases (cost for profit, marked price for discount) are the main trap.

steps.title: Cost of Q from the ratio
steps.body: Cost of P : cost of Q $= 3 : 4$ and the cost of P is $5400$. One part is $5400 \div 3 = 1800$, so the cost of Q is $4 \times 1800 = 7200$.

steps.title: Selling price of Q and the discount
steps.body: Profit on Q is $25\%$ of cost: $\text{SP} = 7200 \times 1.25 = 9000$. Marked price is $10000$, so the discount is $10000 - 9000 = 1000$. As a percentage of the marked price: $\frac{1000}{10000} \times 100 = 10$. That is option (C). The marked price of P, $5860$, is not used.

shortcut.body: Q's cost is $\frac43 \times 5400 = 7200$. Add $25\%$, which is a quarter: $7200 + 1800 = 9000$. Discount $1000$ out of $10000$ is $10\%$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $25$. This copies the profit percentage from the table. Profit is measured on cost, discount on marked price, and they are different quantities.
Choosing $12.5$. A discount of $12.5\%$ needs $\text{SP} = 8750$, a cost of $7000$ and a ratio of cost P to cost Q of $5400:7000$, which is not $3:4$.
Choosing $5$. A discount of $5\%$ needs $\text{SP} = 9500$, a cost of $7600$, and that again breaks the $3:4$ ratio with $5400$.

recognize.clues: Profit is given as a percent of cost and discount is asked as a percent of marked price, with a missing cost found from a ratio.
recognize.contrast: Discount percent and profit percent look alike but use different bases: marked price for discount, cost for profit.

check.body: Work from the percentages. $9000 \div 7200 = 1.25$, so the selling price does give a $25\%$ profit on the cost of $7200$. Also $0.9 \times 10000 = 9000$, so a $10\%$ discount on the marked price lands on the same selling price.

questions.stem:
There are five bags each containing identical sets of ten distinct chocolates. One chocolate is picked from each bag.

The probability that at least two chocolates are identical is ______

steps.title: Probability and the complement rule
steps.body: When all outcomes are equally likely, probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes. 'At least two are identical' means one or more repeated kinds. That event is the opposite of 'all five are different'. For any event $E$, $P(E) = 1 - P(\text{not } E)$, which is the complement rule. Counting the opposite is easier here: all-different has a simple count, while 'at least two identical' has many cases (a pair, two pairs, a triple, and so on).
steps.tex: P(\text{at least two identical})=1-P(\text{all five different})

steps.title: Count the outcomes
steps.body: Each bag holds the same $10$ kinds, and each pick has $10$ choices, so the total is $10^5 = 100000$ equally likely outcomes. For all five different, the first pick can be any of $10$ kinds, the second any of the remaining $9$, then $8$, $7$, $6$: $10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 30240$.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: $P(\text{all different}) = \frac{30240}{100000} = 0.3024$. So $P(\text{at least two identical}) = 1 - 0.3024 = 0.6976$, option (C). A brute-force count over all $10^5$ outcomes gives the same number.

shortcut.body: Multiply the fractions as you go: $1 \times 0.9 \times 0.8 \times 0.7 \times 0.6 = 0.3024$ is the chance all differ; subtract from $1$. Option (A) is exactly $0.3024$, so it is the lure, and the answer is its complement. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $0.3024$. This is the probability that all five chocolates are different, the complement of the event asked. The question asks for at least two identical.
Choosing $0.4235$. It does not come from the count: $1 - 0.4235 = 0.5765$ would need $57650$ all-different outcomes out of $100000$, but there are only $30240$.
Choosing $0.8125$. It would need only $18750$ all-different outcomes. The real count $10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6$ is $30240$, so the probability is $0.6976$.

recognize.clues: The phrase at least two identical covers many cases, while the opposite, all different, has one clean count. Picks from separate bags are independent.
recognize.contrast: This is not a counting-with-repetition question for the favourable event directly: pairs, triples and mixed cases would all need their own counts.

check.body: Build the chance step by step instead of by counting: the second pick avoids the first with chance $0.9$, the third avoids both with $0.8$, and so on. The product must equal the count over the total, a second route to the same value.

questions.stem:
There are multiple routes to reach from node 1 to node 2, as shown in the network.

The cost of travel on an edge between two nodes is given in rupees. Nodes 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', and 'f' are toll booths. The toll price at toll booths marked 'a' and 'e' is Rs. 200, and is Rs. 100 for the other toll booths. Which is the cheapest route from node 1 to node 2?
questions.figure: A directed network from node 1 to node 2 with edge costs in rupees: 1 to a 200; a to c 100; a to 2 200; c to 2 100; 1 to b 300; b to 2 200; b to d 0; d to e 100; e to 2 200; 1 to f 100; f to b 0; f to e 100. Booths a and e charge Rs. 200 and booths b, c, d, f charge Rs. 100.

diagram.alt: Directed network from node 1 to node 2 through nodes a, b, c, d, e, f with the edge costs written on each arrow

solutionDiagram.alt: The four listed routes priced with edge costs plus tolls: 1-a-c-2 costs 700, 1-f-b-2 costs 500 and is cheapest, 1-b-2 costs 600, 1-f-e-2 costs 700

steps.title: How a route is priced
steps.body: The network is a set of nodes joined by arrows; you may only travel along an arrow in its direction. A route from $1$ to $2$ is a chain of arrows. Its cost is the sum of the costs of its edges plus the toll of every toll booth it passes through. Nodes $1$ and $2$ are not booths. The booths $a$ and $e$ charge Rs. 200, and $b, c, d, f$ charge Rs. 100. The cheapest route is the one with the smallest total, so we price each candidate separately: edge costs first, then tolls, then add.

steps.title: Check the routes that are not options
steps.body: Other routes only cost more: 1-a-2 is $200 + 200 + 200 = 600$; 1-b-d-e-2 is $300 + 0 + 100 + 200 + 100 + 100 + 200 = 1000$; 1-f-b-d-e-2 is $900$. The smallest total anywhere is $500$, on 1-f-b-2, option (B). The drawing marks it in bold with the tolls on each booth.

shortcut.body: The Rs. 200 booths $a$ and $e$ are the expensive ones. Routes that avoid both are only 1-b-2 and 1-f-b-2, and the second uses the free edge $f \to b$. Price those two: $600$ and $500$. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 1-a-c-2. Its edges look cheap ($100$ each in the middle), but it passes the Rs. 200 booth $a$ and the total is $700$.
Choosing 1-b-2. It has the fewest edges, but the first edge costs $300$ and the booth $b$ adds $100$. The total is $600$, Rs. 100 more than 1-f-b-2.
Choosing 1-f-e-2. It reaches $2$ through the Rs. 200 booth $e$ and then the Rs. 200 edge $e \to 2$. The total is $700$.

recognize.clues: The question gives a network drawing with edge costs and separate toll charges at marked booths, and asks for the cheapest of four named routes.
recognize.contrast: This is not a shortest-distance problem: the edge costs alone mislead, because the booth tolls change the ranking. Add both before comparing.

check.body: Re-add the winning route in a different order: the tolls of f and b first (100 + 100), then its three edges (100 + 0 + 200). The total matches the first sum. The other three named routes come to 700, 600 and 700 by the same two-part count, so none undercuts it.

hints.text: What does one route actually cost you in total? Think about everything you pay along the way, not only the numbers printed on the arrows.
A route is a chain of arrows followed in their direction, and a toll booth charges every route that passes through it.
The cheapest route has the smallest sum of its edge costs plus the tolls of the booths it passes. A cheap-looking edge can hide an expensive booth.
Note which booths charge the higher toll and see which routes avoid them. Price each remaining route in two parts, edges first and tolls second.
The route that goes straight from node 1 to booth b uses an edge of 300 and then an edge of 200, with only booth b to pay. Price it fully and use it as the figure to beat.

variation.stem: A traveller goes from city P to city Q by one of four routes. Route 1 uses edges costing Rs. 100 and Rs. 200 and passes one booth of Rs. 200 and one of Rs. 100. Route 2 uses edges costing Rs. 150, Rs. 0 and Rs. 200 and passes two booths of Rs. 100 each. Route 3 uses edges costing Rs. 300 and Rs. 100 and passes one booth of Rs. 100. Route 4 uses edges costing Rs. 100 and Rs. 100 and passes two booths of Rs. 200 each. Which is the cheapest route?
variation.explanation: Add edges and tolls for each route. Route 1 is 300 + 300 = 600, Route 2 is 350 + 200 = 550, Route 3 is 400 + 100 = 500 and Route 4 is 200 + 400 = 600. Route 4 has the cheapest edges but the dearest tolls, and Route 3 wins on the total.

questions.stem: The figure below shows an annular ring with outer and inner radii as $b$ and $a$, respectively. The annular space has been painted in the form of blue colour circles touching the outer and inner periphery of annular space. If maximum $n$ number of circles can be painted, then the unpainted area available in annular space is ______.
questions.figure: An annular ring (the region between two circles with the same centre) with inner radius a and outer radius b, both marked as radii from the centre. Equal blue circles are painted around the ring, each touching the inner circle and the outer circle, and each touching its neighbours. The number of circles is n.

diagram.alt: Annular ring with inner radius a and outer radius b filled by a ring of equal blue circles that each touch both rims

solutionDiagram.alt: Annulus with one blue circle highlighted: its diameter b minus a spans the ring width, so each circle has area pi times (b minus a) squared over 4

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: An annulus is the region between two circles with the same centre. With inner radius $a$ and outer radius $b$, its area is the big disc minus the small disc: $\pi b^2 - \pi a^2 = \pi(b^2 - a^2)$. The area of a circle of radius $r$ is $\pi r^2$. Unpainted area $=$ area of the annulus $-$ total area of the painted circles. A painted circle touches the inner rim and the outer rim, so its diameter spans the width of the ring.

steps.title: Size of one painted circle
steps.body: The ring is $b - a$ wide, and a circle touching both rims has that width as its diameter. So its radius is $r = \frac{b-a}{2}$ and its area is $\pi \frac{(b-a)^2}{4}$. For $n$ circles the total is $n \cdot \pi \frac{(b-a)^2}{4} = \frac{n}{4}\pi(b-a)^2$.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body: Unpainted area $= \pi\left[(b^2 - a^2) - \frac{n}{4}(b-a)^2\right]$, option (A). Numeric check with $a = 3$, $b = 5$: the ring holds $12$ circles of radius $1$, the ring area is $16\pi$, the circles take $12\pi$, and the formula gives $\pi(16 - 3 \cdot 4) = 4\pi$, which matches $16\pi - 12\pi$.

shortcut.body: Painted area is part of the ring, so the unpainted area must be less than $\pi(b^2 - a^2)$. That kills (C) and (D), which add. Between (A) and (B), the circle has radius $\frac{b-a}{2}$, so its area has the factor $\frac14$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $\pi\left[(b^2-a^2) - n(b-a)^2\right]$. This takes $b - a$ as the radius, so each circle gets area $\pi(b-a)^2$, four times too large. With $a=3$, $b=5$ and $n=12$ it would even be negative.
Choosing the option with $+\frac n4(b-a)^2$. It adds the circles to the ring, which would give an unpainted area bigger than the ring itself.
Choosing the option with $+n(b-a)^2$. It makes both slips together: wrong radius and a plus sign. The unpainted area cannot exceed the ring area $\pi(b^2-a^2)$.

recognize.clues: The figure is a ring between two concentric circles with equal circles touching both rims, and the question asks for a leftover area as a formula in $a$, $b$ and $n$.
recognize.contrast: This is not a circumference or packing-count problem: $n$ is given, so only areas matter. The trap is using the ring width as the radius instead of the diameter.

check.body: Test two boundary cases on the formula. With $n=0$ nothing is painted, and the formula returns the whole ring area $\pi(b^2-a^2)$. With $a=0$, $b=2$ and $n=1$ the single circle has diameter 2 and area $\pi$ inside a disc of area $4\pi$, so $3\pi$ is left, and the formula gives $\pi(4-1)=3\pi$. The option with $n(b-a)^2$ would give $0$ here.

An annulus is a big disc with a smaller disc cut out of the middle, so its area is the difference of two disc areas.
A circle that touches both rims spans the ring from the inner rim to the outer rim. Its area follows from its radius.
Write the radius of one painted circle in terms of $a$ and $b$, square it for the area, multiply by $n$, and subtract from the area of the ring.

variation.stem: An annular ring has inner radius $2$ and outer radius $6$. Six equal circles, each touching the inner rim, the outer rim and its two neighbours, are painted in it without overlapping. What is the unpainted area in the ring?
variation.explanation: Each circle spans the ring width $6-2=4$, so its radius is 2 and its area is $4\pi$. The ring area is $\pi(36-4)=32\pi$ and six circles take $24\pi$, leaving $8\pi$. Forgetting the factor 6 gives $28\pi$, adding the circles gives $56\pi$, and subtracting nothing gives $32\pi$.

questions.stem: Two straight lines are drawn perpendicular to each other in X-Y plane. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the acute angles the straight lines make with the X-axis, then $\alpha + \beta$ is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two perpendicular lines crossing at the origin: the acute angle alpha with the X-axis on the right and beta on the left satisfy alpha plus 90 degrees plus beta equals 180 degrees

steps.title: Terms and the angle rule
steps.body: The angle a line makes with the X-axis is measured at the point where they cross; the acute one is the one below $90^\circ$. Two lines are perpendicular when they cross at $90^\circ$. The rule: angles that sit side by side along a straight line add to $180^\circ$.

steps.title: Add the angles along the X-axis
steps.body: Through the crossing point draw a line parallel to the X-axis; angles with it equal angles with the X-axis. On the right of the point, the first line makes the acute angle $\alpha$ with the positive X direction. Next comes the $90^\circ$ between the two lines. Then the second line makes the acute angle $\beta$ with the negative X direction. Together they fill a straight angle: $\alpha + 90^\circ + \beta = 180^\circ$, so $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$. This is option (B).

steps.title: Check with slopes
steps.body: A line with slope $m = \tan\alpha$ is perpendicular to a line with slope $-\frac{1}{m}$. The acute angle of the second is $\arctan\frac1m = 90^\circ - \alpha$, since $\tan(90^\circ - \alpha) = \cot\alpha$. For $\alpha = 35^\circ$ this gives $\beta = 55^\circ$ and the sum is $90^\circ$ for every choice of $\alpha$.

shortcut.body: Try one case: lines at $45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$. Both make an acute angle of $45^\circ$ with the X-axis, so the sum is $90^\circ$. About 10 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $60^\circ$. It would need the lines to cross at $120^\circ$ or $60^\circ$. Here the crossing angle is the right angle, so the two acute angles are complementary.
Choosing $120^\circ$. It would need the lines to cross at $60^\circ$, since $\alpha + (\text{crossing angle}) + \beta = 180^\circ$. They cross at $90^\circ$.
Choosing $180^\circ$. This forgets the $90^\circ$ between the two lines in the straight-angle sum, as if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ filled the straight angle by themselves.

recognize.clues: Two lines are stated to be perpendicular, and the question asks for a fixed sum of the two acute angles they make with the same axis, so the sum must not depend on where the lines are drawn.
recognize.contrast: This is not a slope computation: no slopes are given. The angle-on-a-straight-line fact settles it without coordinates.

check.body: Take a pair of perpendicular lines at $20^\circ$ and $110^\circ$ from the positive X-axis. The second one makes an acute angle of $70^\circ$ with the axis. The sum of the two acute angles is the same as for the pair at $45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$, so the sum does not depend on the choice of lines.

questions.stem: The total revenue of a company during 2014-2018 is shown in the bar graph. If the total expenditure of the company in each year is 500 million rupees, then the aggregate profit or loss (in percentage) on the total expenditure of the company during 2014-2018 is ______.
questions.figure: Bar graph of revenue in million rupees for the years 2014 to 2018. The bar heights are 2014: 500, 2015: 700, 2016: 800, 2017: 600, 2018: 400. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 900.

diagram.alt: Bar graph of company revenue in million rupees: 2014 is 500, 2015 is 700, 2016 is 800, 2017 is 600, 2018 is 400

solutionDiagram.alt: Same revenue bars with the 500 million expenditure line dashed; yearly surplus is 0, 200, 300, 100 and minus 100, totalling 500 on 2500 spent

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Revenue is the money coming in and expenditure is the money going out. Profit is revenue minus expenditure, and a negative value is a loss. Profit percent 'on the total expenditure' means profit divided by expenditure, times $100$. 'Aggregate' means the totals over all five years together, not an average of yearly percentages.

steps.title: Read the bars and add
steps.body: Revenue in million rupees: $2014$: $500$, $2015$: $700$, $2016$: $800$, $2017$: $600$, $2018$: $400$. Total revenue $= 3000$. Expenditure is $500$ each year for $5$ years, so $2500$.

steps.title: Compute the percentage
steps.body: Profit $= 3000 - 2500 = 500$, a gain because revenue is more than expenditure. Percentage on expenditure: $\frac{500}{2500} \times 100 = 20\%$, a profit. That is option (C). The solution drawing shows the yearly differences from $500$: $0, +200, +300, +100, -100$, with sum $500$.

shortcut.body: Average revenue is $\frac{3000}{5} = 600$ against $500$ spent each year, so profit per year is $100$ on $500$, which is $20\%$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $16.67\%$ profit. This divides the profit $500$ by the total revenue $3000$ instead of by the total expenditure $2500$. The question says 'on the total expenditure'.
Choosing $16.67\%$ loss. It has both the wrong base ($3000$) and the wrong sign: revenue exceeds expenditure, so there is a profit.
Choosing $20\%$ loss. The size is right but the sign is wrong. Total revenue $3000$ is more than total expenditure $2500$, so the company gained.

recognize.clues: The question gives a bar graph of yearly revenue and a flat yearly expenditure, and asks for the aggregate profit or loss as a percentage on total expenditure.
recognize.contrast: This is not an average of five yearly percentages: the words "aggregate" and "on the total expenditure" fix one ratio of totals.

check.body: Take a second route through the ratio of totals. Revenue over expenditure is $3000/2500=1.2$, so revenue is $20\%$ above spending, and above means profit. Dividing by the revenue instead would give $500/3000=16.67\%$, which is the other base and not what the question asks.

Profit is revenue minus expenditure, and a negative result is a loss. Aggregate means the five years are added first.
A percentage "on the expenditure" divides by the expenditure, not by the revenue.

variation.stem: A company spends 400 million rupees every year. Its revenue in million rupees over five years is 300, 500, 700, 600 and 400. What is the aggregate profit or loss as a percentage of the total expenditure?

questions.stem: Two cars start at the same time from the same location and go in the same direction. The speed of the first car is 50 km/h and the speed of the second car is 60 km/h. The number of hours it takes for the distance between the two cars to be 20 km is ______.

steps.title: Relative speed: how fast a gap grows
steps.body: Speed is the distance covered in one hour. When two objects move in the same direction from the same point, the gap between them changes by the difference of their speeds every hour. That difference is the relative speed. (If they moved toward or away from each other, the speeds would add instead.) The rule: time equals gap divided by relative speed.

steps.title: Relative speed of the two cars
steps.body: Both cars leave the same point, so the gap starts at 0 km. Every hour the faster car covers 60 km and the slower one 50 km, so the gap grows by 10 km each hour.

steps.title: Time to reach a 20 km gap
steps.body: The gap must reach 20 km, so divide it by the 10 km gained per hour. Check: after 2 hours the first car is 100 km from the start and the second is 120 km, a gap of 20 km. This is option (B).

shortcut.body: The gap grows 10 km every hour, so 20 km takes 2 hours. Same direction means subtract speeds, never add them. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 1 hour. After one hour the gap is only 10 km, half of what the question asks.
Choosing 3 hours by dividing the faster speed 60 by the 20 km gap. The speed of one car is not the speed at which the gap grows.
Choosing 6 hours by dividing the faster speed 60 by the 10 km gain, mixing up the gap with a car speed. The gap is 20 km, not 60.

recognize.clues: Two cars leave the same point in the same direction at different speeds, and the question asks when the gap between them reaches a given length.
recognize.contrast: This is not the opposite-direction case, where speeds add. Same direction means the speeds subtract.

check.body: Test by distances. After the time you found, compute how far each car has gone from the start and subtract. The difference must be exactly 20 km. After one hour only half that gap exists, which confirms the time is not smaller.

questions.stem: Ten friends planned to share equally the cost of buying a gift for their teacher. When two of them decided not to contribute, each of the other friends had to pay Rs 150 more. The cost of the gift was Rs. ______.

steps.title: Sharing a fixed cost
steps.body: When a cost is shared equally, each person pays the cost divided by the number of payers. The total cost does not change when friends drop out; only the number of payers changes, so each remaining share grows. The rule: share times number of payers equals the cost.

steps.title: Write both shares and their difference
steps.body: Let the cost be $C$ rupees. With 10 payers each pays $C/10$. With 8 payers (two dropped out) each pays $C/8$. The new share is Rs 150 larger.

steps.title: Solve for the cost
steps.body: Put the fractions over the common denominator 40: $\frac{C}{8} - \frac{C}{10} = \frac{5C - 4C}{40} = \frac{C}{40}$. So $C/40 = 150$ and $C = 6000$. Check: 6000 / 10 = 600 each at first, 6000 / 8 = 750 each later, a rise of 150. This is option (C).

shortcut.body: The difference of the two shares is $C/8 - C/10 = C/40$, so $C = 40 \times 150 = 6000$. Or test the options: only 6000 gives shares 600 and 750. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing 666 without testing it. Its shares are 66.6 and 83.25, which differ by about 16.65, nowhere near 150.
Choosing 3000 by multiplying 150 by 10 and by 2. The shares are then 300 and 375, which differ by only 75.
Choosing 12000 by computing $150 \times 10 \times 8$ and forgetting to divide by the 2 dropouts. The shares are 1200 and 1500, which differ by 300, twice the stated 150.

recognize.clues: A fixed total is shared equally, the number of payers falls, and each remaining share rises by a given amount, so the shares vary inversely with the number of payers.
recognize.contrast: This is not a simple proportion: the amount paid per person does not scale with the people leaving. The total stays fixed while the share changes.

check.body: Substitute each option into the shares. The right cost makes the ten-way share and the eight-way share differ by exactly Rs 150, and the shares must be whole rupee amounts. The three other options give differences of about 17, 75 and 300, so only one fits.

questions.stem: In the given diagram, teachers are represented in the triangle, researchers in the circle and administrators in the rectangle. Out of the total number of the people, the percentage of administrators shall be in the range of ______.
questions.figure: Three overlapping shapes, each region labelled with a head count. The triangle (teachers) points downward. The rectangle (administrators) is tall and narrow, and the top of it overlaps the right corner of the triangle. The circle (researchers) overlaps the bottom of the rectangle. The triangle and the circle do not touch. Region counts: inside the triangle only 70; inside both the triangle and the rectangle 10; inside the rectangle only 20; inside both the rectangle and the circle 20; inside the circle only 40.

diagram.alt: Triangle of teachers (70 alone, 10 shared with the rectangle), tall rectangle of administrators (20 alone, 20 shared with the circle), circle of researchers (40 alone)

solutionDiagram.alt: The same figure with the three administrator regions 10, 20 and 20 shaded, giving 50 of 160 people, which is 31.25 percent

steps.title: Reading an overlap diagram
steps.body: Each shape stands for a group of people, and the number written in a region is how many people sit in exactly that region. Where two shapes overlap, those people belong to both groups. So the administrators are everyone inside the rectangle, overlaps included. The rule for a share is: percentage = (people in the group) / (all people) x 100, where all people means every region counted once.

steps.title: Count the administrators
steps.body: The rectangle holds three regions: 10 (shared with the triangle, so also teachers), 20 (rectangle only) and 20 (shared with the circle, so also researchers). Those overlap people are administrators too.

steps.title: Count everyone
steps.body: Add all five regions once each: the triangle alone, the triangle-rectangle overlap, the rectangle alone, the rectangle-circle overlap, and the circle alone. No region is added twice, so there is no double count.

steps.title: Percentage and the range
steps.body: $50/160 = 5/16 = 0.3125$, so 31.25 percent. That lies between 31 and 45, which is option (C).

shortcut.body: Administrators = 10 + 20 + 20 = 50 out of 160. 30% of 160 is 48, and 50 is just above it, so the share is just above 30: option (C). The value sits close to the edge of (B), so compute it rather than eyeballing. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 0 to 15 by counting only the single region labelled 20 (rectangle only, 12.5%) or only the overlap with the triangle (10, 6.25%). Everyone inside the rectangle is an administrator.
Choosing 16 to 30 by counting administrators as 20 + 20 = 40 and leaving out the 10 that overlaps the triangle. That gives 25%, but a teacher who is also an administrator is still an administrator.
Choosing 46 to 60 by dividing 50 by 100, treating the region numbers as percentages. They are head counts, and the total is 160, not 100.

recognize.clues: Three overlapping shapes carry head counts in each region, and the question asks what percentage of all people fall in one shape, answered as a range.
recognize.contrast: This is not a union-of-sets formula problem: the region counts are already exact, so you add regions rather than subtract overlaps.

check.body: Check the boundaries of the range instead of the exact value. The range ends at 31 percent of 160, which is about 49.6 people, and at 45 percent, which is 72 people. The administrator count must lie between these, and the neighbouring ranges must miss it.

questions.stem: In a college, there are three student clubs. Sixty students are only in the Drama club, 80 students are only in the Dance club, 30 students are only in the Maths club, 40 students are in both Drama and Dance clubs, 12 students are in both Dance and Maths clubs, 7 students are in both Drama and Maths clubs, and 2 students are in all the clubs. If 75% of the students in the college are not in any of these clubs, then the total number of students in the college is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three-circle Venn diagram of the Drama, Dance and Maths clubs with region counts 60, 80, 30, 38, 10, 5 and 2 adding to 225, and 675 outside, in a college of 900

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: "Only in the Drama club" means in Drama and in no other club. "In both Drama and Dance" means in at least those two, so it includes the students who are in the Maths club as well. The whole college is split into the students in some club and the students in no club. If 75% are in no club, the other 25% are in at least one club. The rule: total = (students in at least one club) / 0.25.

steps.title: Split the pair counts into exact regions
steps.body: The 2 students in all three clubs are counted inside each pair count. Take them out to get the students in exactly two clubs: Drama and Dance only $40 - 2 = 38$, Dance and Maths only $12 - 2 = 10$, Drama and Maths only $7 - 2 = 5$. (If the pair counts were read as exactly two clubs, the club total would be 231 and the college 924, which is not an option; the answer choices confirm the reading above.)

steps.title: Count the students in at least one club
steps.body: Add the seven regions of the Venn diagram, each exactly once.

steps.title: Scale up to the whole college
steps.body: 225 students are 25% of the college, so the college has $225 / 0.25 = 900$ students and $900 - 225 = 675$ are in no club, which is 75% of 900. This is option (C). Option (D), 225, is only the number inside clubs.

shortcut.body: Union = singles + pairs - 2 x (triple) = (60 + 80 + 30) + (40 + 12 + 7) - 2 x 2 = 225, because the triple is counted three times in the sum and should count once. Then multiply by 4: 900. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 1000. Then 25% is 250 students in clubs, but the regions add up to exactly 225.
Choosing 975. Then 25% is 243.75, not even a whole number of students.
Choosing 225, which is the number of students in the clubs. The question asks for the whole college, where those 225 are only 25%.

recognize.clues: Three clubs with only-counts, pair counts and a triple count, plus a percentage of students in none, point to inclusion and exclusion followed by a scale-up.
recognize.contrast: This is not three disjoint groups: the pair counts include the triple members, so adding them naively counts those students more than once.

check.body: Count a second way, club by club. Drama has $60+40+7-2=105$ students, Dance $80+40+12-2=130$ and Maths $30+12+7-2=47$. Adding gives 282, which counts each pair twice and the triple three times. Subtract the pair counts $59$ and add back the triple $2$: $282-59+2=225$, the same union. Then $0.25\times 900=225$.

A count such as "both Drama and Dance" includes the students who are also in Maths, so the pair counts overlap with the triple count.
The students in at least one club are the singles plus the pairs, with the triple-club students corrected so that they count once, not three times.
First find how many students belong to at least one club. Then use the percentage given for the students outside every club to scale up to the whole college.
If 75 percent belong to no club, then 25 percent belong to at least one. So the number in clubs equals one quarter of the college.

variation.stem: In a school there are three clubs. Forty students are only in Drama, 50 only in Dance and 20 only in Maths. There are 30 students in both Drama and Dance, 10 in both Dance and Maths, and 8 in both Drama and Maths, and 4 students are in all three clubs. If 80% of the students are in none of these clubs, the total number of students in the school is ______.
variation.explanation: The union is $(40+50+20)+(30+10+8)-2\times4=150$, since the triple is counted three times in the sum. These 150 are 20 percent of the school, so the school has $150/0.2=750$ students. Reading the pair counts as exactly-two gives 810, and giving 150 forgets to scale up.

questions.stem: The area of a square is $d$. What is the area of the circle which has the diagonal of the square as its diameter?

solutionDiagram.alt: A square of area d inside a circle through its four corners; the dashed diagonal is the circle diameter, giving radius squared d over 2 and area pi d over 2

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: The diagonal of a square joins two opposite corners. The diameter of a circle is the distance across it through the centre, and the circle's radius $r$ is half of it. Two rules decide the question: the area of a square with side $s$ is $s^2$, and the area of a circle is $\pi r^2$. For the diagonal, Pythagoras on the right triangle formed by two sides gives diagonal$^2 = s^2 + s^2 = 2s^2$.

steps.title: Find the diagonal
steps.body: The square has area $d$, so $s^2 = d$. The diagonal squared is $2s^2 = 2d$.

steps.title: Find the radius and the area
steps.body: The diagonal is the diameter, so $2r = $ diagonal and $(2r)^2 = 2d$, so $4r^2 = 2d$ and $r^2 = d/2$. The circle area is $\pi r^2 = \pi d/2$, option (D). Check with $d = 2$: side $\sqrt2$, diagonal 2, $r = 1$, area $\pi = \frac12 \pi \cdot 2$.

shortcut.body: The circle through the corners has radius squared $= d/2$ (half the square's area), so the circle area is $\pi d/2$. Test $d = 2$ in the options: only $\frac12 \pi d$ gives $\pi$, the area of the unit circle. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing $\pi d$ by using the side $\sqrt{d}$ as the radius, so that $r^2 = d$. The radius is half the diagonal, not the side.
Choosing $\pi d^2$ by treating $d$ as a length (a radius) when $d$ is already an area. Then $\pi d^2$ has units of length to the fourth power.
Choosing $\frac14 \pi d^2$ by treating $d$ as the diameter, so $r = d/2$. But $d$ is the area of the square, not a length.

recognize.clues: The area of a square is given as a letter, not a length, and the circle is tied to the square through its diagonal. Both areas are built from squared lengths, so the side never has to be found.
recognize.contrast: This is not the inscribed circle, whose diameter is the side. Here the diameter is the diagonal, which is longer by a factor of $\sqrt2$, so the circle is twice as large.

check.body: Try a square of side $3$, so $d=9$. Its diagonal is $3\sqrt2$, the radius is $\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}$ and $r^2=\tfrac{18}{4}=4.5$, giving area $4.5\pi$. Half of $\pi d$ is also $4.5\pi$.

questions.stem: What would be the smallest natural number which when divided either by 20 or by 42 or by 76 leaves a remainder of 7 in each case?

steps.title: What a remainder of 7 means
steps.body: Dividing $N$ by $m$ leaves remainder 7 when $N = km + 7$ for some whole number $k$; that is, $N - 7$ is a multiple of $m$. Here the same remainder 7 must come out for $m = 20$, $42$ and $76$, so $N - 7$ must be a multiple of all three numbers. The multiples shared by several numbers are the common multiples, and the smallest positive one is the LCM (least common multiple). The remainder 7 is smaller than each divisor, so it is a valid remainder.

steps.title: Compute the LCM
steps.body: Factor each number into primes: $20 = 2^2 \cdot 5$, $42 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$, $76 = 2^2 \cdot 19$. The LCM takes the highest power of every prime that appears.

steps.title: Add the remainder
steps.body: The smallest $N - 7$ is 7980, so $N = 7980 + 7 = 7987$. Check each divisor: $7987 = 20 \cdot 399 + 7$, $7987 = 42 \cdot 190 + 7$, $7987 = 76 \cdot 105 + 7$. This is option (C). The numbers that work form the list $7987, 15967, 23947, \dots$ (step 7980), so 63847 $= 8 \cdot 7980 + 7$ also works but is not the smallest.

shortcut.body: Find the LCM of 20, 42 and 76, which is 7980, and add 7: 7987. Skip the option-by-option division. A faster check: the answer minus 7 must be a multiple of 7980, so 7987 is the only option below 8000 with that form. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 3047. It leaves remainder 7 for 20 and 76, but $3047 = 42 \cdot 72 + 23$, so it fails for 42.
Choosing 6047. It leaves remainder 7 only for 20; for 42 the remainder is 41 and for 76 it is 43.
Choosing 63847. It is a correct common solution, equal to $8 \cdot 7980 + 7$, but the question asks for the smallest, which is 7987.

check.body: Subtract 7 from each option and test divisibility by 42. The values $3040$ and $6040$ are not multiples of 42, and $63840$ is a multiple but is eight times the LCM, so it is not the smallest. Only $7980$ is divisible by all three divisors with no smaller multiple possible, since the LCM is the least common multiple.

recognize.clues: The same remainder 7 appears for three different divisors, and the question asks for the smallest such natural number. Removing the remainder turns it into a common multiple.
recognize.contrast: It resembles a plain HCF or LCM question, but the remainder 7 must be added back at the end. It is also not a case of different remainders for different divisors, which would need a congruence method.

questions.stem:
What is the missing number in the following sequence?

2, 12, 60, 240, 720, 1440, ______, 0

steps.title: Finding the rule of a number series
steps.body: A number series follows a rule that turns each term into the next one. Look first at the differences between neighbours (a constant difference means an arithmetic progression). If the differences are not constant, look at the ratios of neighbours (a constant ratio means a geometric progression). When the ratios themselves change by a steady amount, the rule is a product of a changing multiplier.

steps.title: Ratios of neighbours
steps.body: Differences are 10, 48, 180, 480, 720: no pattern. Ratios: $12/2 = 6$, $60/12 = 5$, $240/60 = 4$, $720/240 = 3$, $1440/720 = 2$. The multiplier drops by 1 each time.

steps.title: Continue the pattern
steps.body: The next multiplier is 1, so the blank is $1440 \times 1 = 1440$. The one after is $\times 0$, giving 0, which matches the last printed term. The blank is 1440, option (B).

shortcut.body: The final term is 0, so the last multiplier is 0, and the multipliers go 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, then 1, then 0. The blank is 1440 x 1. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 2880 by repeating the last multiplier 2. The multiplier drops by 1 each step, so after 2 comes 1.
Choosing 720 by expecting the series to fall back symmetrically after the peak. The terms never decrease until the final multiplier 0.
Choosing 0 because the last printed term is 0. The blank sits before it, and 1440 times the multiplier 0 gives the 0 that follows the blank.

recognize.clues: The terms grow fast and the differences are irregular, which points to a product rule. The final term is $0$, which says that the last multiplier is $0$.
recognize.contrast: A geometric progression has one fixed ratio and an arithmetic one has a fixed difference. Here neither is fixed, but the ratios form an arithmetic progression of their own.

check.body: Put each option in the blank and take the neighbour ratios. With 2880 the ratios run $\ldots,2,2,0$, so the multiplier 2 repeats instead of falling by 1. With 720 the ratio is $\tfrac12$, which breaks the whole-number run. With $0$ the next ratio is $0/0$, which is undefined. With 1440 the ratios run $\ldots,2,1,0$ and fall by 1 throughout.

questions.stem: In appreciation of the social improvements completed in a town, a wealthy philanthropist decided to gift Rs 750 to each male senior citizen in the town and Rs 1000 to each female senior citizen. Altogether, there were 300 senior citizens eligible for this gift. However, only 8/9th of the eligible men and 2/3rd of the eligible women claimed the gift. How much money (in Rupees) did the philanthropist give away in total?

steps.title: Money paid = claimants x gift
steps.body: The philanthropist pays only the people who claim. So the total is (number of men who claimed) x Rs 750 plus (number of women who claimed) x Rs 1000. A fraction like 8/9 of the eligible men means the number of men who claimed is $\frac89$ of the number eligible. The split of the 300 between men and women is not given, so look for a way that does not need it.

steps.title: Expected payout per eligible person
steps.body: Write $m$ for the eligible men and $w$ for the eligible women, with $m + w = 300$. Each eligible man brings in $\frac89 \times 750 = \frac{2000}{3}$ rupees on average, and each eligible woman brings in $\frac23 \times 1000 = \frac{2000}{3}$ rupees. The two are equal, so the split does not matter.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: Every one of the 300 eligible people contributes Rs 2000/3, so the total is $300 \times \frac{2000}{3} = 200000$, option (B). Check with 180 men and 120 women: 160 men claim, $160 \times 750 = 120000$; 80 women claim, $80 \times 1000 = 80000$; sum 200000.

shortcut.body: Notice that $750 \times 8/9$ and $1000 \times 2/3$ are both 2000/3, so the men-women split cancels. Total $= 300 \times 2000/3 = 200000$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing 1,50,000 by giving everyone the Rs 750 gift and applying only the 2/3 claim rate: $300 \times 750 \times \frac23 = 150000$. Women get Rs 1000, and the men claim at 8/9.

Choosing 1,75,000 by averaging the gifts to Rs 875 for all 300 people and applying only 2/3: $300 \times 875 \times \frac23 = 175000$. Men and women have different claim rates and different gifts, so averaging them mixes up the two groups.
Choosing 1,51,000. No consistent calculation produces it; it is a near neighbour of 1,50,000. Once the split cancels, the total must be exactly $300 \times 2000/3 = 200000$.

recognize.clues: Two groups with different gifts and different claim fractions, but only the combined size 300 is given. The missing split is a hint that it cancels.
recognize.contrast: A mixture problem usually needs the ratio of the parts. Here the weighted average of the two groups is the same for both, so the ratio is never needed.

check.body: Test the two extremes. If all 300 were men, the cost is $300\times\tfrac89\times750=200000$. If all 300 were women, it is $300\times\tfrac23\times1000=200000$. Both end points agree, so every split in between gives the same total.

questions.stem: If $pqr \neq 0$ and $p^{-x} = \frac{1}{q}$, $q^{-y} = \frac{1}{r}$, $r^{-z} = \frac{1}{p}$, what is the value of the product $xyz$?

steps.title: Exponent rules
steps.body: A negative exponent means a reciprocal: $a^{-x} = 1/a^x$. So $p^{-x} = 1/q$ says $1/p^x = 1/q$, which gives $p^x = q$. The other rule used here: raising a power to a power multiplies the exponents, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$. And if $a^u = a^v$ with $a > 0$ and $a \ne 1$, then $u = v$.

steps.title: Rewrite each condition without negative signs
steps.body: The three conditions become three plain power relations that chain around a loop.
steps.tex: p^{x} = q, \qquad q^{y} = r, \qquad r^{z} = p

steps.title: Substitute around the loop
steps.body: Start from $p = r^z$. Replace $r$ by $q^y$, then $q$ by $p^x$: $p = (q^y)^z = q^{yz} = (p^x)^{yz} = p^{xyz}$. So $p^1 = p^{xyz}$ and, for a base that is not 1, $xyz = 1$, option (C). Numeric check: $p = 2$, $q = 4$, $r = 16$ give $x = 2$, $y = 2$, $z = 1/4$ since $16^{1/4} = 2$, and $xyz = 1$. (If $p = 1$ then $q = r = 1$ and $x, y, z$ are unrestricted; the question intends the ordinary case.)

shortcut.body: Take $p = 2$, $q = 4$, $r = 16$: $2^{-2} = 1/4$, $4^{-2} = 1/16$, $16^{-1/4} = 1/2$, so $x = 2$, $y = 2$, $z = 1/4$ and $xyz = 1$. One numeric example kills (A), (B) and (D) at once. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $-1$ by reading $p^{-x} = 1/q$ as $p^{x} = 1/q$ and dropping the minus signs in all three conditions, which flips the sign of each of $x$, $y$, $z$ and gives $(-1)^3 = -1$.
Choosing $\frac{1}{pqr}$ because the right-hand sides contain $q$, $r$ and $p$. The exponents satisfy a loop that closes on $p$ itself, so the letters cancel.
Choosing $pqr$ by multiplying the three equations side by side. The left sides give $p^{-x}q^{-y}r^{-z} = 1/(pqr)$, which says nothing about the product $xyz$ of the exponents.

recognize.clues: Three conditions that form a loop: $p$ leads to $q$, $q$ to $r$ and $r$ back to $p$. The unknown is a product of exponents, which comes from chaining power-of-a-power steps.
recognize.contrast: Multiplying the three equations together gives a product of bases, not exponents. To get $xyz$ you must substitute so that the exponents multiply, or take logarithms.

check.body: Take logarithms. The conditions become $x\ln p=\ln q$, $y\ln q=\ln r$ and $z\ln r=\ln p$. Multiplying all three, the product $\ln p\ln q\ln r$ appears on both sides and cancels if it is nonzero, leaving $xyz$ alone.
check.tex: xyz\,\ln p\,\ln q\,\ln r=\ln q\,\ln r\,\ln p

questions.stem: In a party, 60% of the invited guests are male and 40% are female. If 80% of the invited guests attended the party and if all the invited female guests attended, what would be the ratio of males to females among the attendees in the party?

steps.title: Percentages of one whole
steps.body: A percentage is a share out of 100 of the same whole. Here the whole is the number of invited guests. Because only the shares matter, you may pretend there are exactly 100 invited guests, so that each percentage is the same as a head count. A ratio of males to females compares the two counts of attendees, not the invited shares.

steps.title: Invited and attending
steps.body: Of 100 invited, 60 are male and 40 are female. All 40 women attend. In total 80 attend, so the number of men who attend is the rest.

steps.title: The ratio
steps.body: Males to females among attendees is $40 : 40 = 1 : 1$, option (B).

shortcut.body: Take 100 guests: 40 women all attend, 80 attend, so 40 men. Ratio 1:1. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 2:3, which flips the invited ratio 3:2 (60 men to 40 women). Even the right way round, 3:2 describes who was invited, not who attended.
Choosing 3:2, which is the ratio of the invited guests (60:40). Not every man attended, so the attendee ratio changes.
Choosing 2:1 from $80 : 40$, using all 80 attendees as the number of men. The 80 includes the 40 women.

recognize.clues: Shares of one group (invited guests) are given along with an attendance percentage, and the ratio asked is for a different group (attendees). A fixed total of 100 turns the shares into counts.
recognize.contrast: A ratio of the original shares, men to women invited, is a different quantity from the ratio among attendees. Only the second one is asked.

check.body: Use a different total of $200$ invited. There are $120$ men and $80$ women, and $160$ attend. All $80$ women come, so $80$ men come, and only two thirds of the men attended. The ratio is still $80:80$.

questions.stem: In the figure below, $\angle DEC + \angle BFC$ is equal to ______ .
questions.figure: Four straight line segments. E to A is the left side, with the point D on it between E and A. E to B passes through the point C, with C between E and B. A to F is the bottom side, with the point B on it between A and F. D to F passes through C, with C between D and F. So the lines E-B and D-F cross at C, and A, B, C, D are the four corners of a quadrilateral. A is the lowest point on the left, F is the far right point and E is the top.

diagram.alt: Lines E to A through D, E to B through C, A to F through B, and D to F through C; E is at the top, A at the bottom left, F at the right

solutionDiagram.alt: The same figure with the angles marked: e at E, f at F, a at A, b at B, c at C and d at D, with the angle chase that gives e plus f equals c minus a

steps.title: Angle facts used
steps.body: $\angle XYZ$ means the angle at the middle letter $Y$, between the rays $YX$ and $YZ$. Two facts decide the question. The three angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. Two angles that sit side by side on a straight line add to $180^\circ$. Since D lies on the line EA and C on the line EB, $\angle DEC$ is simply the angle at E of triangle EAB. Since B lies on AF and C on DF, $\angle BFC$ is the angle at F of triangle BCF.

steps.title: Name the angles
steps.body: Write $e = \angle DEC$, $f = \angle BFC$, $a = \angle BAD$, $b = \angle CBA$ and $c = \angle BCD$. Triangle EAB has angles $e$, $a$ and $b$, so $e = 180 - a - b$.

steps.title: Angle f from triangle BCF
steps.body: In triangle BCF, the angle at C is $\angle BCF = 180 - c$, because D, C, F lie on a line. The angle at B is $\angle CBF = 180 - b$, because A, B, F lie on a line. The three angles add to 180, so $f + (180 - c) + (180 - b) = 180$, which gives $f = b + c - 180$.

steps.title: Add and match
steps.body: Add the two results: $e + f = (180 - a - b) + (b + c - 180) = c - a$. That is $\angle BCD - \angle BAD$, option (A). Numeric check on a sample figure with these lines: $e + f = 57.9^\circ$ and $c - a = 57.9^\circ$, while the other three options give $122.1^\circ$, $208.9^\circ$ and $151.1^\circ$.
steps.tex: \angle DEC + \angle BFC = e + f = c - a = \angle BCD - \angle BAD

shortcut.body: Use the triangles EAB and FAD, which share the angle $a$ at A, and the quadrilateral ABCD. Triangle sums give $e + a + b = 180$ and $f + a + d = 180$, so $e + f = 360 - 2a - b - d$. The quadrilateral gives $b + d = 360 - a - c$. Substituting, $e + f = c - a$. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing $\angle BAD + \angle BCF$. The angle $\angle BCF$ is the supplement of $\angle BCD$ ($180 - c$), so this sum equals $a + 180 - c = 180 - (c - a)$, the supplement of the answer rather than the answer.
Choosing $\angle BAD + \angle BCD$ by adding where the chase subtracts. The angle at A appears in the triangle sums and is removed from the angle at C, so the result is $c - a$, not $c + a$.
Choosing $\angle CBA + \angle ADC$. These are the other two corners of the quadrilateral, $b + d = 360 - a - c$, an intermediate step before subtracting from 360.

recognize.clues: Two extended sides of a quadrilateral meet at E and F, and the question asks for a sum of angles at those points in terms of quadrilateral angles. Triangle sums and straight lines are the only tools.
recognize.contrast: This is not a circle-angle question: no circle or cyclic property is given. The angle at B simply cancels between the two triangle equations.

check.body: Place the quadrilateral on coordinates $A=(0,0)$, $B=(6,0)$, $C=(4,3)$, $D=(1,4)$ and extend the sides so they meet at E and F. Then $\angle BAD\approx76.0^\circ$, $\angle BCD\approx142.1^\circ$ and the two angles at E and F add to about $66.2^\circ$, which equals the difference of the first two.

questions.stem: A six sided unbiased die with four green faces and two red faces is rolled seven times. Which of the following combinations is the most likely outcome of the experiment?
options: Three green faces and four red faces.
Four green faces and three red faces.
Five green faces and two red faces.
Six green faces and one red face.

solutionDiagram.alt: Bar chart of the weights C(7,k) times 2^k for k = 0 to 7 green faces: 1, 14, 84, 280, 560, 672, 448, 128; five green faces is the tallest bar

steps.title: Binomial trials
steps.body: Each roll is an independent trial with two outcomes. An unbiased die lands on a green face with probability $p = 4/6 = 2/3$ and on a red face with probability $1/3$. For $n$ independent trials, the probability of exactly $k$ greens is the number of ways to pick which $k$ rolls are green, times the probability of one such sequence. The question asks which count of greens is the most likely.

steps.title: The formula for seven rolls
steps.body: With $n = 7$, a sequence with $k$ greens has probability $(2/3)^k (1/3)^{7-k} = 2^k / 3^7$, and there are $\binom{7}{k}$ such sequences. The common denominator $3^7 = 2187$ makes the comparison easy: compare $\binom{7}{k} 2^k$.

steps.title: Evaluate the four options
steps.body: $k = 3$: $35 \times 8 = 280$. $k = 4$: $35 \times 16 = 560$. $k = 5$: $21 \times 32 = 672$. $k = 6$: $7 \times 64 = 448$. The largest is 672 at $k = 5$ (probability $672/2187 \approx 0.307$), so five greens and two reds is the most likely: option (C).

steps.title: Why it peaks at 5
steps.body: The most likely count of a binomial is $\lfloor (n+1)p \rfloor = \lfloor 8 \times 2/3 \rfloor = \lfloor 5.33 \rfloor = 5$. The ratio $P(5)/P(4) = \frac{7-4}{5} \times 2 = 1.2 > 1$ and $P(6)/P(5) = \frac{7-5}{6} \times 2 = 0.67 < 1$, so the probabilities rise up to 5 and fall after.

shortcut.body: The mode of a binomial is $\lfloor (n+1)p \rfloor = \lfloor 8 \times \frac23 \rfloor = 5$. Or note the mean $7 \times 2/3 = 4.67$ and compare only 4 and 5: $P(5)/P(4) = 1.2$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing three greens by reasoning as though the die were fair (mean 3.5). Four of the six faces are green, so greens are the more common colour.
Choosing four greens because the mean number of greens, $7 \times 2/3 = 4.67$, sits near 4. The most likely count is not the rounded mean: the weights are 560 for four greens and 672 for five.
Choosing six greens because green is the more likely colour on each roll. Having all but one roll green needs a very specific split; its weight is 448, below 672.

recognize.clues: A fixed number of independent trials with the same chance each time, and the question asks which count is most likely. That is the mode of a binomial.
recognize.contrast: The most likely count is not simply the expected value rounded, and it is not the all-green outcome. Compare neighbouring probabilities directly.

check.body: The weights $\binom{7}{k}2^k$ for $k=0$ to $7$ are $1,14,84,280,560,672,448,128$, and they must add to $3^7=2187$ because the cases are complete. They add correctly, so the weights are right and the largest one is the mode.
