questions.stem: A test has twenty questions worth 100 marks in total. There are two types of questions. Multiple choice questions are worth 3 marks each and essay questions are worth 11 marks each. How many multiple choice questions does the exam have?

steps.title: Two unknowns, two facts
steps.body: The test has two kinds of questions, so there are two unknown counts: let $m$ be the number of multiple choice questions and $e$ the number of essay questions. The question gives two facts, and each fact becomes one equation. The first fact counts questions, the second counts marks. A mark total is (count of a kind) x (marks per question), added over the kinds.

steps.title: Write the equations
steps.body: There are 20 questions in all, and the marks add to 100.

steps.title: Solve
steps.body: From the first equation $e = 20 - m$. Put it in the second: $3m + 11(20 - m) = 100$, so $220 - 8m = 100$, so $8m = 120$ and $m = 15$. Then $e = 5$. Check: $15 \times 3 = 45$ and $5 \times 11 = 55$, total 100. This is option (B).

shortcut.body: If all 20 were multiple choice the test would be worth 60 marks. Each essay in place of a multiple choice adds $11 - 3 = 8$ marks, and 40 more marks are needed, so 5 essays and 15 multiple choice. About 45 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 12 without checking the marks: $12 \times 3 + 8 \times 11 = 124$, not 100.
Choosing 18: $18 \times 3 + 2 \times 11 = 76$. The test needs more essay questions than that.
Choosing 19, leaving only one essay: $19 \times 3 + 11 = 68$. Check any option against the total marks before choosing.

recognize.clues: Two kinds of item with different values (3 marks and 11 marks), a known total number of items and a known total value. These are the two facts that fix two unknown counts.
recognize.contrast: This is not a ratio question, because no ratio of the two counts is given. It is also not alligation of rates; here the totals are exact counts and marks, so two equations solve it directly.

check.body: Test the other options against the 100 total. With 12 multiple choice questions there are 8 essays and the marks are $36+88=124$. With 18 there are 2 essays and the marks are $54+22=76$. With 19 there is 1 essay and the marks are $57+11=68$. None of them gives 100.

questions.stem: There are 3 red socks, 4 green socks and 3 blue socks. You choose 2 socks. The probability that they are of the same colour is

steps.title: Classical probability
steps.body: When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is (favourable outcomes) / (all outcomes). Choosing 2 socks at once means the order does not matter, so each outcome is a pair of socks, and the number of pairs from $n$ socks is $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$. The event 'same colour' is the union of three separate events: both red, both green, both blue.

steps.title: All outcomes
steps.body: There are 10 socks, so there are $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ equally likely pairs.

steps.title: Favourable outcomes
steps.body: Both red: $\binom32 = 3$. Both green: $\binom42 = 6$. Both blue: $\binom32 = 3$. These events cannot happen together, so add them: $3 + 6 + 3 = 12$.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body: $12/45 = 4/15$, option (D). A check with one sock after another: $\frac{3}{10}\cdot\frac{2}{9} + \frac{4}{10}\cdot\frac{3}{9} + \frac{3}{10}\cdot\frac{2}{9} = \frac{24}{90} = \frac{4}{15}$.

shortcut.body: Count same-colour pairs 3 + 6 + 3 = 12 out of 45 pairs, giving 12/45 = 4/15. Since there are 45 equally likely pairs, any correct answer has the form $k/45$, which already rules out $1/4$ and $7/30$. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $1/5 = 9/45$ by counting same-colour pairs for only two of the three colours (3 + 6 = 9), leaving out one of the two groups of 3 pairs (red or blue).
Choosing $7/30$. It is not a multiple of $1/45$ ($7/30 = 10.5/45$), so no count of pairs can give it.
Choosing $1/4$. It would need 11.25 favourable pairs out of 45, impossible for a count.

recognize.clues: Two socks are chosen from a small set with known colour counts, and the event is that the colours agree. Everything is equally likely, so favourable pairs over all pairs applies.
recognize.contrast: Choosing both together is a pair count. Drawing one sock after another gives the same value, but it needs conditional chances at each draw, which is the longer route here.

check.body: Draw one sock after another without replacement. The second sock must match the first, so multiply the chance of each colour first by the chance of the same colour next, then add. The three terms sum to the same fraction as the pair count.

questions.stem: X is a 30 digit number starting with the digit 4 followed by the digit 7. Then the number $X^3$ will have

steps.title: Digits and powers of ten
steps.body: A positive whole number has $k$ digits exactly when it is at least $10^{k-1}$ and below $10^{k}$. For example, 100 has 3 digits because $10^2 \le 100 < 10^3$. So X having 30 digits starting with 47 means X lies in a window between two numbers of the form 47000...0 and 48000...0.

steps.title: The window for X
steps.body: X begins with the digits 47 and has 30 digits, so it is at least $4.7 \times 10^{29}$ and below $4.8 \times 10^{29}$.

steps.title: Count digits
steps.body: A number of the form $1.\ldots \times 10^{89}$ is at least $10^{89}$ and below $10^{90}$, so it has $89 + 1 = 90$ digits. This is option (A). A 30-digit number cubed can have at most 90 digits whatever its leading digits.

shortcut.body: Every 30-digit number is below $10^{30}$, so its cube is below $10^{90}$ and has at most 90 digits; that removes (B), (C) and (D) at once. A 30-digit number has a cube with 88 to 90 digits, and $4.7^3 \approx 104 > 100$ pushes it to 90. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing 91 digits by adding one after tripling: $3 \times 30 + 1$. A 30-digit number is below $10^{30}$, so its cube is below $10^{90}$ and has at most 90 digits.
Choosing 92 digits. This is impossible: the cube of any 30-digit number is below $10^{90}$.
Choosing 93 digits by tripling the digit count and then adding the exponent 3 ($30 \times 3 + 3$). A digit count is not an exponent: the cube of a 30-digit number is below $10^{90}$.

recognize.clues: The number of digits of a power is asked, and the first digits of the base are given. The leading digits decide whether the cube crosses a power of ten.
recognize.contrast: Without the leading digits only a range of digit counts is possible. The leading digits turn the range into one value, so bounding the cube is needed rather than just multiplying 30 by 3.

check.body: Use logarithms. The base ten log of $X$ lies between $\log_{10}4.7+29$ and $\log_{10}4.8+29$, that is about 29.67 to 29.68. Tripling gives about 89.01 to 89.04, and a log with whole part 89 means 90 digits.

questions.stem: The number of roots of $e^x + 0.5x^2 - 2 = 0$ in the range $[-5, 5]$ is

solutionDiagram.alt: Graph of f(x) = e^x + 0.5 x^2 - 2 on -5 to 5: a bowl shape with lowest point about -1.27 at x = -0.57, crossing zero at x about -1.93 and x about 0.60

steps.title: Roots, sign changes and curve shape
steps.body: A root of $f(x)$ is a value of $x$ where $f(x) = 0$, that is, where the graph of $f$ meets the horizontal axis. Two facts decide how many there are. First, if a continuous function is positive at one point and negative at another, its graph must cross the axis somewhere between them. Second, a curve that always bends upward (a bowl shape, convex) can cross the axis at most twice.

steps.title: Find the sign changes
steps.body: Let $f(x) = e^x + 0.5x^2 - 2$. Then $f(-5) = 10.51 > 0$, $f(-1) = -1.13 < 0$, $f(0) = -1 < 0$ and $f(1) = 1.22 > 0$. The sign changes from plus to minus between $-5$ and $-1$, and from minus to plus between $0$ and $1$, so there are at least two roots.

steps.title: At most two roots
steps.body: The second derivative is $f''(x) = e^x + 1 > 0$ for every $x$, so $f$ is convex and a bowl. The slope $f'(x) = e^x + x$ is increasing, so it is zero at one place only ($x \approx -0.57$, where $f \approx -1.27$). The curve falls to this lowest point and then rises, so it crosses zero at most twice.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: At least two and at most two, so exactly two roots, at about $x = -1.93$ and $x = 0.60$, both inside $[-5, 5]$. This is option (C).

shortcut.body: Check signs at three points: $f(-5) > 0$, $f(0) = -1 < 0$, $f(5) > 0$. That is two sign changes, so at least 2 roots. $f'' = e^x + 1 > 0$ makes the graph a bowl, so at most 2. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing 0 because every term of $e^x + 0.5x^2$ looks positive. The constant $-2$ drops the curve below zero near $x = 0$, where $f(0) = -1$.
Choosing 1 after finding only the root between 0 and 1. On the negative side $e^x$ is small, but $0.5x^2$ reaches 2 near $x = -2$, so the curve crosses again near $-1.93$.
Choosing 3 by solving $0.5x^2 = 2$, which gives $x = \pm 2$, and then adding a root from $e^x$. But $f(2) = 7.4 > 0$ and $f$ is a bowl that crosses the axis only twice.

recognize.clues: The number of zeros of a mixed exponential and quadratic is asked over a fixed interval. Plot-reading ideas apply: sign changes give a lower bound and curve shape gives an upper bound.
recognize.contrast: Solving the equation algebraically is not possible because the exponential and the quadratic mix. Counting crossings from the shape of the graph is the method, not solving for $x$.

check.body: Count sign changes of $f(x)=e^x+0.5x^2-2$ at whole numbers. $f(-2)\approx0.14>0$, $f(-1)\approx-1.13<0$, $f(0)=-1<0$ and $f(1)\approx1.22>0$. The sign flips once between $-2$ and $-1$ and once between $0$ and $1$. Both ends $f(\pm5)$ are large and positive, so no further flip is hidden.

questions.stem:
An air pressure contour line joins locations in a region having the same atmospheric pressure. The following is an air pressure contour plot of a geographical region. Contour lines are shown at 0.05 bar intervals in this plot.

If the possibility of a thunderstorm is given by how fast air pressure rises or drops over a region, which of the following regions is most likely to have a thunderstorm?
questions.figure: A rectangular map with contour lines labelled in bar (0.65, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95) and four regions marked by pink circles. R is at the top left where the 0.65 line and the 0.7 line run almost on top of each other, nearly touching. P is on the left, on the tight innermost 0.95 loop of a set of nested closed loops around a pressure peak (0.9 and further loops outside it). S is on the right, on the tight 0.95 loop of another set of nested loops (0.9 around it). Q is at the bottom centre, its circle on the 0.8 line, with the 0.75 line further below. A scale bar shows 0, 1 and 2 km.

diagram.alt: Sketch of the contour map with the regions R at the top left between tightly packed 0.65 and 0.7 lines, P and S on tight nested loops, and Q on the 0.8 line with the 0.75 line far below

solutionDiagram.alt: The contour sketch with the gap between neighbouring lines marked at each region: smallest at R, closer than Q's at P and S, widest at Q, so R has the steepest pressure change

steps.title: What contour lines tell you
steps.body: A contour line joins places with the same pressure. Neighbouring lines here differ by the same step, 0.05 bar. The distance between two neighbouring lines is the gap. The pressure change per kilometre is (0.05 bar) / (gap in km). Every pair of lines has the same 0.05 on top, so a smaller gap means a faster change in pressure. The question defines thunderstorm risk as exactly this speed of change.

steps.title: Read the gaps at each region
steps.body: At R the 0.65 and 0.7 lines run side by side, almost touching: the smallest gap on the map. P and S each sit on tight nested loops, closer than Q's gap but wider than R's, and a peak's top is nearly flat. Q sits on the 0.8 line with the 0.75 line far below: the biggest gap to its next line, so the calmest pressure.

steps.title: Rank and answer
steps.body: Gap from smallest to largest: R, then P and S, then Q. So the pressure changes fastest at R, which is option (C).

shortcut.body: Look for where the contour lines crowd together; that is where pressure changes fastest. The lines at R almost merge. About 20 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing P because nested loops look busy. The loops around P are spaced far wider than the 0.65 and 0.7 lines at R.
Choosing Q because it sits next to the 0.8 line. Q lies in the widest gap on the map, so the pressure there changes slowly.
Choosing S for the same reason as P: tight nested loops around a peak, still wider than the gap at R.

recognize.clues: A contour map with a fixed interval between lines and a question about how fast a quantity changes. The spacing of the lines is the quantity to compare.
recognize.contrast: A peak or a loop is not the same as a steep slope. A set of loops can be widely spaced, so the spacing between lines at the marked point, not the loop shape, decides.

check.body: Compare R with Q on the map. Each crosses exactly one 0.05 bar step, R between the 0.65 and 0.7 lines and Q between the 0.75 and 0.8 lines, so the top of the fraction is the same. The ratio of their rates is then the inverse ratio of their gaps, and because R's gap is the smaller one, R's rate is the larger.

questions.stem: Find the smallest number $y$ such that $y \times 162$ is a perfect cube.

steps.title: Perfect cubes and prime exponents
steps.body: A perfect cube is a whole number of the form $n^3$, such as $8 = 2^3$ or $27 = 3^3$. Every whole number above 1 splits into primes in exactly one way, for example $72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$, and the small raised number on each prime is its exponent. Cubing a number triples every exponent, so a number is a perfect cube exactly when every prime in it has an exponent that is a multiple of 3 (0, 3, 6, 9, ...). That one rule decides the question: multiply 162 by the smallest $y$ that lifts each exponent up to the next multiple of 3.

steps.title: Factor 162
steps.body: Divide by primes: $162 = 2 \times 81 = 2 \times 3^4$. The prime 2 has exponent 1 and the prime 3 has exponent 4. Neither is a multiple of 3, so 162 is not a cube.

steps.title: Lift each exponent to a multiple of 3
steps.body: The exponent of 2 must rise from 1 to 3, so $y$ needs two more factors of 2. The exponent of 3 must rise from 4 to 6, so $y$ needs two more factors of 3. Any other prime in $y$ would only make $y$ larger without helping, so the smallest choice is $y = 2^2 \times 3^2$.

steps.title: Check and match
steps.body: $36 \times 162 = 5832 = 2^3 \times 3^6 = (2 \times 3^2)^3 = 18^3$, a perfect cube. The answer is 36, option (D).

shortcut.body: Factor 162 as $2 \times 3^4$. Round each exponent up to a multiple of 3: 2 needs $2^2$ more and 3 needs $3^2$ more, so $y = 4 \times 9 = 36$. Only option (D) is divisible by both 4 and 9. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing 24 = $2^3 \times 3$. It makes the exponent of 2 a multiple of 3 by adding a whole cube of 2 instead of the missing two factors, and it leaves $24 \times 162 = 2^4 \times 3^5$, with exponents 4 and 5.
Choosing 27 = $3^3$ because 162 contains a power of 3 and 27 is a cube. Multiplying by a cube never repairs the exponents: $27 \times 162 = 2 \times 3^7$, and the exponent of 2 is still 1.
Choosing 32 = $2^5$ after fixing only the prime 2. The result $2^6 \times 3^4$ has a cube in 2 but the exponent 4 on 3 is still not a multiple of 3.

recognize.clues: A smallest multiplier that makes a product a perfect cube. Perfect powers are decided by the exponents in the prime factorisation.
recognize.contrast: Making a perfect square needs even exponents, and a cube needs multiples of 3. Multiplying by a cube changes nothing about the gaps, so the multiplier is the product of the missing prime copies, not a cube.

check.body: Try the smaller multipliers. Since $162=2\cdot3^4$, a multiplier of 12 gives $2^3\cdot3^5$ and the exponent of 3 is 5, not a multiple of 3. A multiplier of 18 gives $2^2\cdot3^6$ and the exponent of 2 is 2. Each falls short, so a multiplier needs both a $2^2$ and a $3^2$, which is 36.

variation.explanation: Factor $180=2^2\times3^2\times5$. The exponents 2, 2, 1 must rise to 3, 3, 3, so $y$ needs one more 2, one more 3 and two more 5s: $y=2\times3\times25=150$. The number 30 only adds one of each prime, which leaves the exponent of 5 at 2.

questions.stem: The probability that a $k$-digit number does NOT contain the digits 0, 5, or 9 is
questions.keyNote: Read literally, a k-digit number cannot start with 0, so the exact probability is $7^k / (9 \cdot 10^{k-1}) = \tfrac{10}{9}(0.7)^k$, which the enumeration script confirms for k = 1 to 4 and which matches none of the options. The official key C uses the digit-by-digit reading, where every position is any of the ten digits; $0.7^k$ is then exact and is the only option of that form.

steps.title: Probability and independent positions
steps.body: The probability of an event is the number of outcomes that satisfy it divided by the number of equally likely outcomes. A $k$-digit number has $k$ positions, and each position holds one of the ten digits 0 to 9. Two choices are independent when one does not change the options of the other. For independent choices, the chance that all of them satisfy a condition is the product of the chances for each one. So the plan is: find the chance that one position avoids 0, 5 and 9, then multiply $k$ copies.

steps.title: One position
steps.body: Of the ten digits, three are forbidden (0, 5 and 9), so seven are allowed: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8. The chance that one position is allowed is $7/10 = 0.7$.

steps.title: All k positions
steps.body: The question says the number must not contain the three digits anywhere, so every position must be allowed. The positions are independent, so the chances multiply: $0.7 \times 0.7 \times \cdots \times 0.7$ with $k$ factors. As a count, $7^k$ allowed strings out of $10^k$ strings.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: The result $0.7^k$ is option (C). The options $0.3^k$, $0.6^k$ and $0.9^k$ would need 3, 6 or 9 allowed digits per position out of ten, and the allowed count is 7. A strict reading that forbids a leading zero changes the total to $9 \times 10^{k-1}$ and gives $\tfrac{10}{9}(0.7)^k$, a value no option shows; the intended answer is the digit-by-digit one.

shortcut.body: Count allowed digits per position: 10 minus 3 forbidden is 7, so 0.7 per position and $0.7^k$ for $k$ positions. The other options need 3, 6 or 9 allowed digits, which cannot be. About 20 seconds. The shortcut is unsafe only if an option carried the exact $\tfrac{10}{9}$ factor for the leading digit.

traps.text: Choosing $0.3^k$, the chance that every digit is one of the three forbidden digits. It answers the opposite question; the complement of a single digit being forbidden is $0.7$, not $0.3$.
Choosing $0.6^k$ by counting six allowed digits, one fewer than the true seven. Remove exactly the three listed digits from the ten and no more.
Choosing $0.9^k$ after excluding only one digit per position, for example thinking only the digit 0 matters because a number cannot start with 0. The digits 5 and 9 are forbidden as well.

recognize.clues: A condition on every digit position of a $k$-digit number, with the same rule at each position. Repeated independent positions turn one chance into a power.
recognize.contrast: This asks for all positions to avoid the forbidden digits, not for at least one to contain them. The complement form is a different question with the answer $1-$ this power.

check.body: Cross-check with the complement. For $k=1$ the forbidden digits are 0, 5 and 9, which is $3/10$, and $1-0.3=0.7$. For $k=2$ the strings with at least one forbidden digit number $30+30-9=51$ by inclusion and exclusion, so the clean strings are $100-51=49=7^2$.

questions.stem: The expression $\dfrac{(x+y)-|x-y|}{2}$ is equal to

steps.title: Absolute value and the one rule
steps.body: The absolute value $|a|$ is the distance of $a$ from 0: it equals $a$ when $a \ge 0$ and $-a$ when $a < 0$. So $|x-y|$ is the gap between $x$ and $y$ on the number line, and it is never negative. Which of the two forms applies depends only on which of $x$ and $y$ is larger. The rule that decides the question is therefore to split into two cases, $x \ge y$ and $x < y$, remove the bars in each, and see what is left. The maximum of two numbers is the larger one and the minimum is the smaller one.

steps.title: Case x at least y
steps.body: Here $x - y \ge 0$, so $|x-y| = x-y$. The numerator is $(x+y)-(x-y) = 2y$, and dividing by 2 leaves $y$. In this case $y$ is the smaller number.

steps.title: Case x less than y
steps.body: Here $x - y < 0$, so $|x-y| = -(x-y) = y-x$. The numerator is $(x+y)-(y-x) = 2x$, and dividing by 2 leaves $x$. In this case $x$ is the smaller number.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: In both cases the expression equals the smaller of the two numbers, so it is the minimum of $x$ and $y$: option (B). Test with $x = 3$, $y = 7$: $(10-4)/2 = 3$. With $x = 7$, $y = 3$ the value is again 3.

shortcut.body: Plug in two different numbers, $x = 3$ and $y = 7$: $(10-4)/2 = 3$, the smaller one. That rules out the maximum (7), the constant 1 and, since the value is the same for $x=7$, $y=3$, "none of the above". Use unequal values, because for $x = y$ both the minimum and the maximum agree. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing the maximum, which is the value of $\dfrac{(x+y)+|x-y|}{2}$. Here the bars are subtracted, which removes the gap and leaves the smaller number.
Choosing 1 after trying $x = y = 1$, where the expression is indeed 1. One equal pair does not prove a general rule; with $x = 3$, $y = 7$ the value is 3.
Choosing "none of the above" because the result seems to depend on which number is larger. It does depend on the case, but both cases give the same description, the smaller number.

recognize.clues: The expression is the average of $x$ and $y$ combined with half of $|x-y|$, their gap. The average pushed down by half the gap lands on an endpoint.
recognize.contrast: Adding the half gap in place of subtracting gives the other endpoint. The sign in front of the absolute value is what separates the minimum from the maximum.

check.body: Test cases the solution did not use: equal numbers and a negative one. With $x=y=5$ the absolute value is 0 and the expression is $10/2=5$, which is the smaller of the two equal numbers. With $x=-2$, $y=4$ it is $(2-6)/2=-2$, again the smaller number, and the larger one, 4, is not what comes out.

questions.stem: Arun, Gulab, Neel and Shweta must choose one shirt each from a pile of four shirts coloured red, pink, blue and white respectively. Arun dislikes the colour red and Shweta dislikes the colour white. Gulab and Neel like all the colours. In how many different ways can they choose the shirts so that no one has a shirt with a colour he or she dislikes?

solutionDiagram.alt: Grid of Arun, Gulab, Neel and Shweta against red, pink, blue and white with Arun-red and Shweta-white crossed, and the count by Arun's shirt: white gives 6, pink gives 4, blue gives 4, total 14

steps.title: Arrangements and restrictions
steps.body: Four people take four different shirts, one each, so a way to choose is an arrangement of the four shirts among the four people. With no restriction there are $4! = 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ arrangements: 4 shirts for the first person, 3 left for the next, and so on. A restriction removes the arrangements that give a person a disliked colour. The rule used here is to split by the case that controls the restriction (Arun's shirt), count each case with the multiplication rule, and add the cases, which never overlap.

steps.title: Set up the two restrictions
steps.body: Arun may not take red, and Shweta may not take white. Gulab and Neel may take anything. In the grid of the drawing the two crossed cells are the forbidden pairs (Arun, red) and (Shweta, white).

steps.title: Case: Arun takes white
steps.body: Then white is gone, so Shweta's restriction cannot be broken. The remaining three shirts (red, pink, blue) go to Gulab, Neel and Shweta in any order: $3! = 6$ ways.

steps.title: Cases: Arun takes pink or blue
steps.body: Say Arun takes pink. The remaining shirts are red, blue and white. Shweta must avoid white, so she has 2 choices (red or blue). Gulab and Neel then take the two shirts left in $2! = 2$ ways. That is $2 \times 2 = 4$ ways. Arun taking blue is the same, another 4 ways.

steps.title: Add the cases
steps.body: The three cases are different choices for Arun, so they share no arrangement. The total is $6 + 4 + 4 = 14$, option (D). The same number comes from inclusion-exclusion: 24 arrangements, minus 6 with Arun in red, minus 6 with Shweta in white, plus the 2 counted twice with both, giving $24-6-6+2$.

shortcut.body: Inclusion-exclusion: fix one person in a forbidden shirt and arrange the other three, $3! = 6$ ways; both people forbidden at once leaves $2! = 2$. So $24 - 6 - 6 + 2 = 14$. About 1 minute. The method is safe because the two restrictions are about different shirts and different people.

traps.text: Choosing 21 = 24 - 3 by removing only 3 arrangements for a restriction. Fixing Arun in red leaves the other three people free to take the other three shirts in $3! = 6$ ways, not 3.
Choosing 18 = 24 - 6 by applying only one restriction, Arun's. Shweta's dislike of white must be removed too.

Choosing 16 by starting from the 18 left after Arun's restriction and removing only the 2 arrangements that break both rules. Shweta in white removes 6 arrangements in total, and 2 of them were already gone, so only $6 - 2 = 4$ more go: $18 - 4 = 14$.

recognize.clues: Four people take four different shirts, one each, and two of them have a forbidden colour. "Different ways" with a restriction on specific person-shirt pairs points to counting arrangements and removing the bad ones.
recognize.contrast: This is not a plain permutation count: without the dislikes there would be $4!$ ways. It is also not a count of independent choices, because a shirt taken by one person is unavailable to the next.

check.body: Count the bad arrangements directly. Arun in red can be completed in $3!$ ways, Shweta in white in $3!$ ways, and both together in $2!$ ways, so the bad ones number $6+6-2=10$ and the good ones $24-10$. A second route splits on Shweta instead of Arun: if Shweta takes red, the other three people share pink, blue and white with Arun avoiding nothing new, which gives 6 ways; if she takes pink or blue, Arun still must avoid red, which gives 4 ways each. The totals agree.

questions.stem: A contour line joins locations having the same height above the mean sea level. The following is a contour plot of a geographical region. Contour lines are shown at 25 m intervals in this plot. If in a flood, the water level rises to 525 m, which of the villages P, Q, R, S, T get submerged?
questions.figure: A rectangular map with five villages marked by red dots. Left half: a hill drawn as nested closed contour lines around P. From the outside in, the lines are an outer line running off the bottom of the map, the line labelled 500, a line just inside it, the line labelled 550, and a small innermost closed loop with P on it. Village R sits in the low ground at the top centre, outside the outermost line of the left hill and outside the lines of the right hill. Right half: a second hill. A long line labelled 500 runs from the top of the map down the left side of the hill, curves along its bottom and leaves at the right edge. Inside it a second line starts at the top edge, curves down and round and leaves at the right edge too, so it encloses the whole top-right corner, where Q is marked. Inside that, a closed ring labelled 550 and a smaller closed loop inside the ring. Village T lies at the right edge between the second line and the line labelled 500. Bottom right: a small closed loop near the bottom edge with a still smaller loop labelled 450 in it, and village S inside the outer loop. Top left: two open lines labelled 425 and 450. Contour lines are 25 m apart.

diagram.alt: Contour map with nested lines around P on the left hill, lines labelled 500 and 550 on both hills, R in low ground at top centre, Q in the top-right corner, T at the right edge below the right hill, and S inside small loops at the bottom right

solutionDiagram.alt: The contour map with every line labelled in metres and the 525 m lines in blue; R, S and T lie outside the 525 m lines at heights below 525 m and are submerged, while P and Q lie inside them and stay dry

steps.title: Contour lines and a flood level
steps.body: A contour line joins all points of the same height above sea level, so walking along one line you never climb or descend. Neighbouring lines differ by the same step, here 25 m. Going from a line towards the middle of a closed ring of lines, the ground rises by 25 m per line; going out, it falls. A village standing between two lines has a height between those two values. A flood to 525 m covers every place whose height is below 525 m. So the rule is: a village is submerged exactly when it lies on the low side of the 525 m line.

steps.title: Label the lines
steps.body: Use the printed labels and the 25 m step. On the left hill the lines from the outside in are 475, 500 (labelled), 525, 550 (labelled) and an innermost loop at 575. On the right hill the long line labelled 500 is outermost, then the 525 line that runs from the top edge to the right edge, then the ring labelled 550, then an inner loop at 575. The two 525 lines are the flood line, drawn in blue in the solution drawing.

steps.title: Read each village
steps.body: P is inside the ring labelled 550, on the innermost loop, so it is above 550 m. Q is in the top-right corner, inside the 525 line and next to the 550 ring, so it is above 525 m. R is in the low ground outside the 500 lines of both hills, so it is below 500 m. S lies inside the small loop group at the bottom right, whose innermost loop is labelled 450, so its levels are 450 or lower and never above 500 m; S is outside every 500 line. T lies between the long line labelled 500 and the 525 line, so its height is between 500 m and 525 m.

steps.title: Apply the flood level
steps.body: Submerged means height below 525 m. P and Q are above it and stay dry. R, S and T are below it and go under. The submerged villages are R, S, T: option (C).

shortcut.body: Find the 525 lines (the ones between the labels 500 and 550). Whatever lies outside them is under water. P sits at the top of the left hill, high and dry, which removes (A) and (B). Options (C) and (D) then differ only in T against Q: Q is inside the 525 line and T is outside it, so (C). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing P, Q, the villages that stay dry. This reads the flood backwards: water covers the low ground, not the peaks.
Choosing P, Q, T by taking the two high villages P and Q as submerged and adding T. P is above 550 m and Q is above 525 m, so neither can be under a 525 m flood.
Choosing Q, R, S by swapping T and Q. Q lies inside the 525 line in the corner by the 550 ring; T lies outside it, between the 500 line and the 525 line, so T floods and Q does not.

recognize.clues: The question gives contour lines at a fixed 25 m interval, a few labelled values, and a water level of 525 m. Reading a village's height from the lines around it is the skill being tested.
recognize.contrast: This is not a data-interpretation question over a table or bar chart: there are no plotted values to read off an axis. The heights come only from counting lines away from a labelled line and using the step size.

check.body: Count instead of tracing lines. Five villages are named and exactly two, P and Q, sit inside the 525 line, so a flood to 525 m must leave three under water. Only option (C) lists three villages, and they are the three left outside the 525 line. Now substitute heights: the lowest dry village, Q, is above 525, so it is not covered, while the highest submerged one, T, is below 525, so it is covered.
